t.thracian tomb of kazanlak@42.6,25.4:
In 1944 soldiers digging a shelter on the edge of Kazanlak broke into a small brick chamber and found themselves looking at some of the finest ancient paintings in the Balkans. The Thracian Tomb of Kazanlak, built in the fourth century BC for a ruler of the Thracians, has a narrow corridor leading to a round, beehive-shaped burial chamber, its dome covered with frescoes of a funeral feast: the dead man and his wife seated at a table, servants bringing gifts, horses and chariots racing around the top. The colours and the tenderness of the figures are extraordinary. It was listed by UNESCO in 1979.

The original tomb is closed to protect the paintings, but a full-size replica nearby lets you see them in detail. The real tomb lies under a mound in a park on the hill above the town, and there are many more Thracian burial mounds in the surrounding area, in what is called the Valley of the Thracian Kings. Several have been excavated and can be visited, and the ruins of Seuthopolis, a Thracian city, lie beneath the waters of a reservoir nearby.

Kazanlak sits in the Valley of Roses, between the Balkan Mountains to the north and the Sredna Gora to the south. For centuries the valley has grown roses for their oil, used in perfumes around the world, and in late May and early June the fields bloom pink and the air is heavy with scent. The town holds a rose festival at that time, with parades, music and the crowning of a Rose Queen. The rose museum explains the history of the industry.

The riding nearby is superb. North of the town, the road climbs over the Shipka Pass, scene of fierce battles in the Russo-Turkish War of 1877 to 1878, which led to Bulgaria's liberation from Ottoman rule. At the top stands the Freedom Monument, and on the way up you pass the golden domes of the Russian memorial church at Shipka village. Nearby, on another peak, is Buzludzha, a huge, abandoned communist monument shaped like a flying saucer. The roads are winding, with good views and variable surfaces.

Kazanlak has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try rose jam, rose liqueur, or a Bulgarian salad with white cheese. Summers are hot, winters cold, with snow on the passes. Early June is the best time to visit, when the roses are in bloom.
t.terioki@60.2,29.7:
Terioki, or Terijoki in Finnish, is the old name of Zelenogorsk, a resort town on the northern shore of the Gulf of Finland, about fifty kilometres from St Petersburg. Until the Winter War, it was part of Finland, and before the revolution it was one of the favourite dacha destinations for the wealthy of the imperial capital, who came by train to spend summers among the pine trees and sandy beaches. After the Soviet Union took the Karelian Isthmus in 1940 and again in 1944, the Finnish population left, and in 1948 the town was renamed Zelenogorsk, the green hill.

The town still has traces of its former life. A few wooden villas from the early twentieth century survive along the shady streets, and the church of the Kazan Icon of the Mother of God, built shortly before the First World War, stands in the centre with its distinctive domes. There is also an old Finnish Lutheran church. The beach is wide, sandy and shallow, with long views over the gulf to Kronstadt on clear days, and in summer it fills with families from the city.

The riding is gentle. The coastal road from St Petersburg, the Primorskoye shosse, runs along the shore through Repino, Komarovo and Zelenogorsk, with pine forest on one side and the sea glimpsed on the other. It is mostly straight with gentle bends, and on summer weekends it is clogged with traffic heading to the beaches. Weekday mornings are much better. The faster motorway, the Scandinavia highway towards Vyborg, runs inland. Repino is home to the Penates, the house of the painter Ilya Repin, now a museum, and Komarovo is known for its cemetery where the poet Anna Akhmatova is buried.

The landscape is typical of the Karelian Isthmus: pine and birch forest on sandy soil, lakes, bogs and granite boulders left by the ice sheets. In June, the white nights mean daylight lasts almost around the clock, and the light on the gulf in the late evening is soft and silvery.

Zelenogorsk has fuel, shops and cafés. Bear in mind that conditions for foreign travellers in Russia have changed considerably; check visa, insurance and travel advice carefully before planning a trip, and expect payment cards issued abroad not to work.
t.the maritime channel@60.0,29.6:
Stand on the shore anywhere near Kronstadt and you are looking at a dredged highway hidden under the water. The Maritime Channel, the Sea Canal of St Petersburg, was cut through the shallow Neva Bay in the late nineteenth century, opening in 1885, so that large ships could reach the city's port directly instead of unloading at Kronstadt. Before it existed, the bay was too shallow for anything but small vessels, and cargo had to be transferred to lighters, a slow and expensive business. The channel runs for around thirty kilometres from the open gulf to the mouth of the Neva, marked by buoys and lights, and it remains the main artery for ships entering the city.

The island of Kotlin, with the naval town of Kronstadt, sits at the western end of the bay. Peter the Great founded the fortress there in the early eighteenth century to protect his new capital from the Swedish fleet, and it became the base of the Baltic Fleet. The Naval Cathedral of St Nicholas, completed in 1913, dominates the town with its huge dome, and the harbours and forts around the island tell three centuries of naval history.

Today Kronstadt is connected to both shores of the gulf by the flood protection barrier, a chain of dams and sluices completed in 2011 to protect St Petersburg from the storm surges that have flooded the city repeatedly over its history. The ring road runs along the barrier, crossing the main shipping passage through a tunnel beneath it. Riding across is a strange experience: a motorway in the middle of the sea, with water on both sides and the wind blowing hard and constantly. Crosswinds can be strong, so hold on.

The landscape is flat and open, all sky and water. Seabirds gather on the rocks of the old forts, and in winter the bay freezes and fishermen walk out on the ice. The light changes constantly, from steel grey to brilliant blue, and sunsets over the gulf in summer last for hours.

Kronstadt has fuel, shops and cafés, and the towns on the southern shore, Lomonosov and Peterhof, are close. As for any trip in Russia at present, check entry requirements and travel advice carefully before you go.
t.aalto campus@62.2,25.7:
Alvar Aalto grew up in Jyväskylä, and the city wears his work like a signature. The university campus on the hill of Seminaarinmäki is one of his great achievements, designed in the 1950s around the older buildings of the teacher training college that had stood here since the nineteenth century. Red brick, timber, copper and glass, arranged around a sloping green with tall pines, it feels less like an institution than a village built for thinking. The main building, with its grand stair and lecture hall, the library and the sports hall all carry his particular mix of warmth and rigour. Walk around and you notice the details: the door handles, the light, the way the buildings follow the slope.

The city has a museum dedicated to him, also designed by Aalto, and there are more of his buildings scattered around Jyväskylä and its surroundings. Säynätsalo Town Hall, a short ride south, is one of his masterpieces, a small brick civic building arranged around a raised courtyard. On the island of Muuratsalo, nearby, is the Experimental House, his summer home, where he tested materials and ideas on its brick walls.

Jyväskylä is a university town on the shores of Lake Jyväsjärvi in the Finnish Lakeland, and the landscape around it is classic Finland: forests of pine, spruce and birch, countless lakes, granite outcrops, and roads that ripple up and down over glacial ridges. The riding is relaxed and scenic rather than technical. The roads are generally well maintained, with gentle curves, and traffic is light outside the city. The great lake Päijänne, one of the largest in Finland, stretches south, and the roads along its shores offer endless views of water and islands.

A few practical notes. Finland has strict speed limits and plenty of fixed cameras, and fines are calculated on income, so they can be eye-watering. Watch for elk and deer, especially at dawn and dusk; warning signs mean what they say. The riding season is short, from May to September, and summer brings long light evenings when you can ride until nearly midnight.

The city has fuel, cafés and restaurants, and a sauna by the lake is easy to find. Finish the day as Finns do: in the heat, then in the water.
t.fort krasnaya gorka@60.0,29.3:
On the southern shore of the Gulf of Finland, near the village of Lebyazhye, the remains of Fort Krasnaya Gorka sit among pine woods and sand dunes. The fort was built in the years before the First World War as part of a chain of coastal defences protecting the approaches to St Petersburg, with heavy guns facing the sea and their counterparts on the opposite shore at Ino, in what was then the Grand Duchy of Finland. Together, the forts were designed to close the gulf to an enemy fleet.

Krasnaya Gorka is remembered for two episodes. In June 1919, during the Civil War, its garrison mutinied against the Bolsheviks; the uprising was crushed within days, with battleships from Kronstadt shelling the fort. In the Second World War, the fort was part of the Oranienbaum bridgehead, a pocket of territory on the southern shore that held out against the German army throughout the siege of Leningrad, and its guns supported the defence of the city. After the war the fort was gradually abandoned, and today concrete batteries, bunkers and gun emplacements lie overgrown in the forest, with a small museum and memorials nearby.

The landscape is typical of the southern coast: pine forest on sandy ground, dunes and boulders on the shore, and wide views over the gulf. On calm summer days the water is pale and still, and you can see across to the northern shore; in autumn, storms send waves crashing against the boulders.

The riding is calm. The coastal road from Lomonosov to Sosnovy Bor runs through villages and forest with gentle curves and moderate traffic, and the views of the sea come and go between the trees. It is not a road for excitement, but it is pleasant and relaxed, especially in the long evenings of June. Beyond Sosnovy Bor, the road continues west along the coast towards the Estonian border region, with fewer cars and more forest.

Lebyazhye has a few shops, and Sosnovy Bor, a nuclear power station town, has fuel, supermarkets and cafés. The fort itself has no services. As with any trip in Russia at present, check visa requirements, insurance and travel advice carefully, and keep in mind that military sites in this region may have access restrictions.
t.baneasa la cetate@43.9,25.0:
Băneasa is Teleorman, and Teleorman is flat. The Wallachian plain here spreads out between the Danube, to the south, and the lower Vedea valley, with big fields, long horizons and the sort of sky that makes motorcyclists look for any rise at all. The label "La Cetate" marks one such rise, where traces of an old fortification are known locally, and the nearby "Traian - La Culă" name hints at the Roman presence that once ran across this part of southern Romania.

That Roman connection is the story here. In the second century the empire strung a line of earthworks and forts through this region, the Limes Transalutanus, running east of the Olt river toward the Danube plain, to guard the edge of the province of Dacia. Much of it is now just a faint embankment crossing a field, visible when the light is low and the crop is short. I cannot promise a clear ruin at the exact pin, so treat this as a stop for the idea more than the image: the road you are riding is on ground that soldiers once patrolled.

On a bike, the area is undemanding and honest. The country roads are straight, the corners are mostly junctions into villages, and the surface runs from smooth asphalt to something that looks like it lost an argument with a tractor. Wind is the main character, especially in spring and autumn, when it gusts across open ground with nothing to stop it. In July and August the heat is heavy and shade is rare, so start early, carry water and wear light colours. Storks nest on poles in many villages, and watching them circle on warm air is one of the better free entertainments in the south of Romania.

Practical things: Băneasa itself is a small village, and so are Băduleasa and Salcia, though Salcia is slightly bigger and may have a shop. For fuel and a proper meal, aim for Peretu, about seventeen kilometres away, or the larger towns along the main road to the Danube. Gravel and dust can drift across the tarmac near fields after harvest, so go carefully on bends. If you have time, ask any elder in the village about the old fortress; people know their local rises and love to talk about them.
t.the coastal fort reef@60.0,29.6:
In the shallow, grey waters of the Gulf of Finland, a chain of fortified islands guards the sea approach to Saint Petersburg. Peter the Great founded the naval base of Kronstadt on Kotlin Island in 1703, and over the following two centuries forts were built on artificial islets and reefs to the north and south, to form a defensive screen. Fort Reef, called Rif in Russian, is one of these, a low, stone-and-earth structure in the water, and I cannot say what access exists to it today. In many cases the forts are military or ruined, and visits require permission.

Kronstadt itself is a fascinating place. The town, with its straight streets, canals and white-and-gold cathedral built for the navy, was the base of the Russian Baltic Fleet, and in 1921 its sailors rose in rebellion against the Bolsheviks, a revolt crushed by troops crossing the ice. In recent years a dam, completed in 2011 to protect Saint Petersburg from storm surges, has linked Kotlin Island to both shores of the gulf, and a highway runs along the top of it, so you can ride onto the island for the first time without a boat.

The riding is an odd mix. The dam road is a long, straight, modern highway with sea on both sides, and it can be very windy, with spray in rough weather. Elsewhere in the area, roads are flat, with port traffic and heavy lorries, and on Kronstadt itself the streets are quiet and cobbled in places. Summer evenings, with the sun low over the gulf, are lovely, and the white nights of June bring a pale, glowing sky until after midnight. Fog and storms can close the dam.

Kronstadt has fuel and shops, and the main street has cafés and a market, so plan to refuel there or on the mainland. Local food is simple, with fish, soups and pastries. Keep to public areas, avoid photographing military installations, and carry your passport, because security is taken seriously in this region.
t.lindulovskaya roshcha@60.2,29.5:
Out on the Karelian Isthmus, in a landscape of pine, birch and sandy soil, stands a grove of larches that looks entirely out of place. The Lindulovskaya Grove was planted in 1738 by an admiral, Fyodor Soimonov, who wanted to grow shipbuilding timber for the Russian navy, and he chose Siberian larch, a durable and rot-resistant wood. Some of the trees are nearly three centuries old and very tall, and the grove is protected as a natural monument, the oldest planted larch forest in Russia. Walking among the trunks, with their orange-grey bark, and the soft light filtering through the needles, is surprisingly moving.

The isthmus has a complicated history. It was Finnish territory from 1917 until the Winter War of 1939 and 1940, and the villages here once had Finnish names, church towers and farms. After the war the population changed, and the landscape was reshaped by Soviet settlement, with dachas and military sites. In the Second World War the isthmus was a front line, and the Road of Life, the lifeline of besieged Leningrad, which ran across the ice of Lake Ladoga, begins not far north. Memorials and monuments appear at many roadsides.

Riding on the isthmus is different from riding in the city. The roads are wide, often straight, and pass through forests and past lakes, with traffic building on the roads out of Saint Petersburg on Friday afternoon. Surfaces vary, with some very good and some patched. Summer brings mosquitoes and warm evenings, autumn brings mushroom pickers by the road, and winter is long and dark. The best time to visit the grove is late summer and early autumn, when the light is softest and the forest is quiet.

Roshchino, about five kilometres away, has fuel stations, shops and cafés, and Molodezhnoye has a few shops. Local food includes mushroom soup and fish from the lakes. Bring insect repellent for the grove, stay on the paths, and take care not to damage the roots or bark, since the trees are protected.
t.sunila housing area@60.5,27.0:
Alvar Aalto designed this place before the Second World War, and you can still read the plan on the ground. Sunila is a pulp mill on a rocky island near Kotka, on the Gulf of Finland, and Aalto designed both the mill buildings and the housing for the workers, in the late 1930s. The houses step down the slope in terraces among the pines, with an eye for views and shared space, which was unusual for an industrial settlement then. The mill still runs, with smoke rising over the pines on cold mornings, so the place is a working one, not a museum, and the housing area is lived in by residents who deserve some quiet.

The landscape is quintessentially Finnish coast, flat rock, low pines, granite outcrops polished by the ice and shallow bays full of reeds. Kotka itself is a harbour town on a group of islands at the mouth of the Kymijoki river, and it is one of the busiest ports in Finland. It has a good maritime centre, Maretarium, an aquarium of Finnish waters, and the Langinkoski rapids nearby, where a fishing lodge was built for Tsar Alexander III, who liked to fish there. Karhula, on the mainland side, has an old glassworks tradition.

Riding in this corner of Finland is relaxed. The roads are smooth, wide and nearly empty, with speed limits that are strictly enforced, so there is no reason to hurry. The countryside is flat, with long lines of spruce and birch, and in summer the light lasts until ten or later. Beware of elk at dawn and dusk, and of road surfaces that can be rutted after a hard winter. The best months are June to August, with September bringing cool, clear air and autumn colour.

Fuel and food are easy in Kotka and Karhula, both of which have good supermarkets, cafes and petrol stations. Order a plate of vendace or Baltic herring, or a salmon soup, and finish with a cardamom bun. Hamina, fifteen kilometres to the east, is a star-shaped fortress town worth a detour. Bring a jacket, since the sea wind is always colder than you expect.
t.experimental house@62.1,25.7:
Alvar Aalto built himself a summer house here on Muuratsalo, an island in Lake Päijänne's northern waters near Jyväskylä, and called it the Experimental House. He began it in the early 1950s, and the idea was literal: the walls of the square courtyard are patched with dozens of different bricks and tiles, laid out as samples to see how they weathered through Finnish winters. It is a low whitewashed building with a courtyard open to the sky, and it sits between the pines and the water. Nearby, in Säynätsalo, his town hall of dark red brick is a gem of Finnish modernism.

The region is the Finnish Lakeland, a country made of water. Lakes lie in every hollow, and the land between them is covered with spruce, pine and birch, with granite outcrops and boggy meadows. Jyväskylä, fourteen kilometres away, is a university city of some eighty-five thousand with a lot of Aalto buildings in its streets, and a good museum devoted to him. Muurame, a few kilometres closer, has fuel, supermarkets and cafes.

For the rider, the pleasure is calm. The roads are smooth, the bends are gentle, and the traffic is light, apart from the summer weekend when everyone heads to their lake cottages. Bridges link the islands in the Päijänne, and crossing them gives good views over the water. Take it easy, because speed cameras are common and fines in Finland are linked to income. Watch out for elk at dusk. In June the light lasts almost all night, and the midsummer period is magical.

Visiting hours at the house are limited, and access can be restricted, so check in advance. If you miss the opening, the lake and the woods are good consolation. Take a flask, find a flat rock by the shore, and watch the water. Finnish summers have a smell of pine resin and warm lake water that stays with you. The Petäjävesi Old Church, a wooden church from the eighteenth century and also a UNESCO site, lies a short distance away through the forest and makes a good second stop, with a long timber roof like an upturned boat.
t.porlom ii tornikallio@60.7,26.0:
Tornikallio means tower rock in Finnish, and it is a common name for a rocky hill with a view. I cannot tell you what is at this particular spot, but I know the country around it. Artjärvi and Myrskylä lie in the rolling farmland where Uusimaa meets Kymenlaakso, a landscape of small lakes, red barns, rye and oat fields and patches of spruce forest, drained by the Porvoonjoki river on its way to the Gulf of Finland. It is gentler than the lake district farther north, and it has a well-worn look, with old wooden farmhouses and village churches painted white or ochre.

Verla Groundwood and Board Mill, named in one of the ride titles, lies some distance to the east, near Kouvola, and is a UNESCO site since 1996. It is a small, almost perfectly preserved nineteenth-century factory village, where wood was ground into pulp and pressed into cardboard, and the red brick buildings stand around a rapid in the river. It is a good reason to ride this corner of the country, and the mill closed in the 1960s, leaving the machines in place.

The roads here are quiet and fast, with long, well-surfaced straights and a few easy bends, and traffic is light even in summer. Elk are a real danger at dawn and dusk, and the speed limits drop in villages. Gravel side roads are common and usually well graded. The best time is June to August, when the light is long and the fields are green, though September brings clear air and the first autumn colours.

The nearest places are small. Artjärvi has about fifteen hundred people, Myrskylä two thousand, and Lapinjärvi three thousand, so fuel and food are limited. Orimattila, nineteen kilometres away, is the nearest town with a full range of services. Fill the tank there. Look for a village shop with a coffee machine, a cinnamon bun and a bench outside, which is as good as most restaurants. The northern light and a lake on the horizon do the rest.
t.southern battery no 2@60.0,29.7:
Kotlin Island sits in the middle of the Gulf of Finland like a cork in a bottle, and Peter the Great knew it. He seized this stretch of coast from Sweden in 1703 and almost at once began fortifying the island to guard the new capital, Saint Petersburg, which lay at the head of the gulf. Over the next two centuries a ring of forts and batteries grew up on islands, shoals and the shore, and Kronstadt became the home port of the Baltic Fleet. The batteries named in these ride titles, Southern and Northern, belong to that defensive system. I cannot tell you what survives at this spot, and the batteries are often hard to reach, overgrown or fenced off, so treat this as a stop for imagination and a look at the water.

The sea here is shallow and a muddy green, and in winter it freezes so hard that armies have marched across it. The modern landmark is the flood barrier, a long dam with a road on top that was finished in 2011 to protect the city from surge floods, and which now carries the ring road across the water between the mainland north and south shores and Kotlin. Riding it is an odd experience, with open sea on both sides, wind pushing at the bike and the low outline of Kronstadt ahead. Crosswinds can be fierce, and the road is a fast highway shared with heavy lorries.

On the island, Kronstadt itself is a town of about forty-three thousand with a grid of straight streets, a naval cathedral with a gilded dome and a few canals that used to hold the fleet's dry docks. Fuel and food are available there and in Lomonosov, which lies on the opposite shore at a similar distance. The south shore road between Lomonosov and Bolshaya Izhora is quiet and wooded, and good for an easy coastal run.

Travel in Russia has become complicated, and rules for foreign visitors and vehicles can change, so check before planning anything here. If you are able, come on a clear June evening, when the sun hangs low over the gulf for hours and the forts glow orange on the horizon.
t.the barrier of pile@60.0,29.7:
Izhora is an old name for this part of the coast. Long before Saint Petersburg, the land between the Neva and the Luga belonged to the Izhorians, a small Finnic people who fished, farmed and served as pilots on the river, and whose language survives only in a few villages. Bolshaya Izhora, the Great Izhora, is a modest settlement on the shore, with a church, some dachas and a sea wall, and the nearest town of any size is Kronstadt across the water. The point on the map sits at the edge of the gulf, in reed and low scrub, where the shallows run out for hundreds of metres and the horizon is a thin line of cranes and chimneys. I am not sure what the Barrier of Pile referred to here, but a line of timber piles driven into shallow water is a classic way of closing a channel to ships, and this is exactly the sort of coast where one would be used.

The honest summary is that the stop is as much about the landscape as the monument. The sea breeze brings a smell of salt, mud and pine, gulls scream over the shingle, and on a clear day you can see Kronstadt's forts as grey shapes on the water. Fishermen sit on the shore in winter on the ice, drilling holes and waiting patiently with thermos flasks.

The roads along this stretch are flat, quiet and a little rough. The shore road between Bolshaya Izhora and Lomonosov passes through pinewood and small villages, with tarmac that frost has broken in places, and the traffic is local. Weekday mornings are best, and wet weather turns the verges to mud. Do not expect much in the way of fuel in the village. Kronstadt and Lomonosov are the nearest places to fill up, each some ten kilometres away, and both have supermarkets and cafes.

Bring a jacket, since the wind off the water is cool even in July, and take a moment to walk to the shore and watch the sky change. Check current travel rules before going, as conditions for visitors in this region have altered recently.
t.primorskoe highway@60.2,29.6:
Zelenogorsk used to be Terijoki, a Finnish resort town on the Gulf of Finland, and it belonged to Finland until the Winter War of 1939 to 1940, when this stretch of the Karelian Isthmus passed to the Soviet Union. Before that, Terijoki was a place where Russian aristocrats and artists kept summer houses, and the wooden villas that survive among the pines still have some of that air. The Primorskoe highway runs north-west from Saint Petersburg along the shore to Vyborg, and this is the part of it where the road threads a sandy, forested coastal strip with dunes on one side and wet pinewoods on the other. The ride titles link it to the Monastery of Troitse-Sergieva Pustyn, which stands on a different part of the coast; I would not promise you can reach it from this point.

The road is a good one for an easy run. It is wide, mostly well surfaced, and passes through a series of resort settlements, with long straight stretches and a few gentle curves through trees. At weekends it is busy with day trippers and cars heading to dachas, and in summer it can be slow. The best time is early in the morning, when the air smells of resin and the sea glints through the trunks. In winter the sand freezes, the sea becomes a white plain, and the road is sometimes icy.

Zelenogorsk has about fifteen thousand people and has fuel and cafes, while smaller places like Roshchino and Molodezhnoye are near. Between them the forest is thick, and wild blueberries and mushrooms are picked in season by people who park on the shoulder and wander in with baskets. It is a landscape that locals love, and they will tell you which pine has the best view. Watch for crossing elk in the dusk.

The isthmus has a long and heavy history of wars and border changes, and the old Finnish frontier lay not far north. Visitors should check the current rules for entering the area, since they have changed, and the situation near the border can be complicated. If you are able to go, the quiet beach in the evening is the best place to be.
t.traian la cula@43.7,25.0:
Teleorman county is flat. It is the heart of the Romanian Plain, an open expanse of black soil that runs from the Carpathian foothills to the Danube, and from the saddle of a motorcycle it looks like a sea of sunflowers, wheat and maize under a very large sky. Traian, a small village a short ride from Turnu Magurele, sits in the middle of it. The label La Cula refers to a cula, the fortified tower house typical of the Balkans, and the name suggests a past with more upheaval than the quiet fields would suggest.

What makes the place interesting to historians is its position. In the second and third centuries AD, the Romans built a second line of defence, the Limes Transalutanus, a chain of earth ramparts, ditches and small forts that ran across the plain east of the Olt, to guard the province of Dacia from raiders across the river. Traces of these earthworks can still be found in the fields, low humps and long lines that look like nothing until you are told what they are. It is a landscape that rewards imagination more than sightseeing.

For riding, expect long, straight roads, light traffic away from the main routes, and sudden bumps where the pavement has settled. Wind is a constant, and in summer the heat comes in waves, often above thirty-five degrees. Dust and slow farm machinery are normal. The best seasons are May and June, when the crops are green, and September, when the fields are golden and the air is clearer. The Danube is not far away, and Turnu Magurele is a pleasant river town, with a view across the water to Bulgaria, where the town of Nikopol was the scene of a famous medieval battle in 1396, in which a crusader army was defeated by the Ottomans.

Poiana and Ciuperceni are small villages with a basic shop at best, while Turnu Magurele, a town of nearly thirty thousand people, has fuel, supermarkets and cafes. Fill the tank there, bring water, and look for the roadside stalls that sell watermelons in late summer, which are some of the sweetest in the country.
t.vallum troian@44.0,25.0:
The Romanian word vallum is a Latin leftover, and it means a rampart. Across the plain north of the Danube, in Teleorman county, a line of low earthworks stretches over the fields, and local people call it Troianul, Trajan's ditch, though no one is sure whether Trajan had anything to do with it. Folk memory has also attached the name of Novac, a legendary hero, to the same banks, and archaeologists suggest the line may have formed part of a Roman or late Roman defence of the Wallachian Plain, though the dating remains debated. What you will find on the ground is subtle: a long, shallow hump in a wheat field, a line of poplars following an old ditch.

The setting is the real reward. This is the broad, flat Danubian plain, with villages like Baneasa, Salcia and Tudor Vladimirescu spaced out along straight roads lined with walnut trees. Houses are painted in bright colours, gates are carved or wrought iron, and storks build huge nests on the telephone poles, which in summer are full of noisy chicks. Sunflowers fill the horizon in July, and in September the maize is harvested and the air smells of dust and dry stalks. Time seems to move at the speed of a tractor.

The riding is straightforward, with flat, long roads, fast in places but often broken by potholes, and the occasional horse-drawn cart. Wind can be strong, and summer temperatures are often high, so plan for early starts and long breaks at midday. Spring, when the fields are bright green and the poppies are in flower, is the nicest time. In winter, the plain is bleak and cold, with fog and sometimes ice.

Villages here generally have a shop and a bar where men gather for beer and cards, and some of the larger ones, such as Salcia, will probably have a petrol pump, though I would not count on it. Peretu, fourteen kilometres away, is the larger town on the map, and Alexandria, the county capital, has everything you might need. Carry water, and accept the offer of coffee, which is usually strong, sweet and served in tiny cups.
t.thracian tomb of sveshtari@43.7,26.8:
In a quiet corner of the Ludogorie, the wooded plateau of north-eastern Bulgaria, a grassy mound hides one of the most remarkable tombs in the Balkans. Sveshtari is a Thracian tomb of the Getae, a tribe that lived on both sides of the lower Danube, and it dates from the third century BC. Over the burial chamber, the builders raised a mound, and inside they built a stone vestibule, a corridor and three chambers, decorated with carved and painted figures, the likes of which are not found anywhere else in the Thracian world. UNESCO listed it in 1985.

The most striking feature is the ten female figures in the central chamber, carved in half-relief on the walls, with their arms raised, and holding up the architrave like caryatids. They are crowned with flowers and look like goddesses or priestesses. On the ceiling, painted murals show a woman being welcomed by a horseman, which may represent the dead ruler's wife entering the afterlife, or the goddess greeting the hero. The interior is extremely fragile, so access is limited, with small groups led by a guide and with timing rules that vary by season, so it is wise to check before you go. It is a profoundly peaceful and strange place.

The Ludogorie is gentle riding country, with low hills, beech and oak woods, fields of sunflowers and wheat, and villages with storks on the chimneys. Roads are generally flat or rolling, the surface is mixed, and traffic is light. The name means mad forest, a reference to the dense woods that once covered the area. The nearby Srebarna lake, a wetland on the Danube, is a haven for pelicans and herons, and the Madara Rider, a medieval relief carved in a cliff, lies not far to the east.

Isperih, six kilometres away, is a small town with fuel, shops and cafes, and Zavet is nearby. Summers are hot and dry, with sunflowers at their best in July, and autumn brings the harvest, with grapes and walnuts. Nearby cafes serve Bulgarian yoghurt, grilled meat and a chilled glass of rakia. Carry water, and take time to wander the fields.
t.fort constantin@60.0,29.7:
Fort Constantine sits off the western end of Kotlin Island, out in the Gulf of Finland, and the sea is the whole point of it. Kotlin is a long, thin strip of land with the island city of Kronstadt at its heart, built by Peter the Great as the base of the Baltic fleet and the shield for St Petersburg. The forts around it were built on shoals and artificial islands to close the channels, which means several of them can only be seen from a distance, or from the water.

Constantine is one of the nineteenth-century coastal forts, from a time when the Russian empire expected attack from British and French fleets. After the Crimean War, when an Allied squadron nosed around the Baltic, the defences were reinforced. The forts are low, long and made of granite and brick, built to sit just above the waterline and present as small a target as possible. Their casemates, parapets and ruined gun emplacements bleach and grow mossy, a little like the bones of some sea creature, and the whole group has a melancholy that photographs rarely catch.

For riding, the flavour of this area is the long coastal approach, flat and straight, with grey water on one side and birch scrub on the other. There are very few corners. It is a ride about distance and sky, and about the cold wind that can shove a bike sideways without warning. Check the forecast before you commit, because fog and sea-spray can make the exposed shoreline unpleasant. Surfaces near the coast suffer from frost and salt, so potholes and patched asphalt are normal.

Kronstadt itself is a naval town with fuel and food. Access to the island and to some of the forts has varied over the years, so it is worth confirming what you can actually reach rather than assuming. The sea air carries salt and the faint smell of weed and diesel. Come in the long light of June or in September, when the water goes a deep slate colour and the old walls turn warm in the evening.
t.northern battery no 3@60.0,29.8:
Kotlin Island is only about twelve kilometres long and rarely more than a kilometre or two wide, and every metre of its northern shore was given over to guns. A numbered battery like this one is the sort of thing that appears on a map as a dull label and turns out to be a lump of overgrown concrete and earth, with ammunition stores half buried in the ground and a view across a shallow, pewter-coloured sea. Kronstadt, four or five kilometres away, was founded by Peter the Great in the first years of the eighteenth century to keep Swedish ships out of the new capital's approaches, and the fortifications grew in layers for the next two hundred years.

What makes these northern defences interesting is that they were obsolete almost as soon as they were finished. Rifled guns, then steel ships, then aircraft kept moving the goalposts, so every generation built another ring and left the old one to rust. Walk the paths and you can read the history in the masonry: granite blocks from the age of sail, red brick from the nineteenth century, grey reinforced concrete from the twentieth. The trees have taken over the earthworks, and in summer the whole thing is green and humming with insects.

Riding here is flat and quiet, a matter of single-lane roads between low fences and scrubby woodland, with sudden gaps that show the water. The surface is patchy, with frost damage and sand blowing across the tarmac near the shore, so treat any corner cautiously. Traffic is light apart from the occasional truck. Wind from the gulf is the main enemy; on a cold day it will find every gap in your jacket.

For fuel and food you want Kronstadt itself, a town of about forty-three thousand with petrol stations and plenty of small cafes. The towns on the mainland, Gorskaya and Aleksandrovskaya, are smaller. Bring a layer even in July, because the sea breeze here can feel like October.
t.the barrier of stone@60.0,29.9:
The Barrier of Stone is a name that sounds like a medieval wall, though what is actually out here is a creature of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries: the great flood barrier that stretches across the Gulf of Finland to protect St Petersburg. The city has been flooded again and again since its foundation, because it sits at the mouth of the Neva on land barely above sea level, and when westerly storms push water up the gulf the river backs up and spills into the streets. The worst floods are remembered in literature, most famously in Pushkin's poem about the bronze horseman.

After decades of argument and long pauses in construction, a complex of dams, gates and navigation passages was completed across the gulf. The structure links the mainland north of the city with Kotlin Island and then runs on south to the other shore, with a ring road running along its top. Riding it is a distinctive experience. The road is wide, dead straight in long sections, and so exposed that you feel the weather in a way you never do on land. A crosswind can lean you a surprising amount, and the water on either side shifts from grey to green to near-black depending on the sky.

There are no hills and almost no bends, so this is not a road for those who want corners. What it offers instead is scale: the low outline of the fortress islands, the cargo ships on the channel, the distant towers of the city. Gulls and cormorants work the water, and in winter the ice makes strange plates and ridges.

Kronstadt, about six kilometres from the point, is the closest real town, and it has fuel, food and a surprisingly rich old centre of naval buildings, a great cathedral and canals. There are fewer services on the barrier itself, so arrive with a tank in good shape. Speed limits are enforced on this stretch, and traffic can be heavy with trucks, so treat it as a serious road and not an afternoon dawdle.
t.the coastal fort shanetz@60.0,29.7:
Shanetz sounds like a word for a small redoubt, and that is roughly what these coastal forts were: low, squat batteries put on islets and spits to cover the fairways into the Gulf of Finland. This one lies in the western approaches of Kotlin, on the shoals north of the island, and it belongs to the great ring of defences that earned Kronstadt its nickname as the key to Petersburg. The forts earned their keep during the Crimean War, when Allied ships came up the Baltic, took a look at the defences and decided not to risk an attack.

Today the site has the look of a place left behind. The brickwork stands in the water, covered in weed and algae, and the casemates are open to the wind. Gulls nest on the parapets. What you notice most, standing near the edge of the shore, is the silence: the sea slapping at stones, the creak of reeds, a faraway ship's engine. In misty light the forts hang in the haze like ships that have run aground.

Approach matters more than technique here. Roads to the coast are narrow and often broken at the edges, with sandy patches that appear without warning, so keep your speed down and watch for loose gravel. The land is flat as a table and the gulf wind reaches you fully. If you have the choice, come on a calm day or in the evening, when the light turns the water to copper.

Kronstadt, a little over six kilometres away, is where you fill the tank and eat. It has around forty-three thousand people, a handful of cafes, a famous dry dock and a sombre history of naval mutiny, most notably the uprising of 1921. Military zones here have opened and closed over the years, so check current information before riding out to a specific point. Take warm layers and a flask, because even a sunny day can turn raw once the wind comes in off the water.
t.srebarna nature reserve@44.1,27.1:
Srebarna is a freshwater lake beside the Danube in the far northeast of Bulgaria, a few kilometres from the Romanian border, and it is one of the most important wetlands in Europe. The lake and its reed beds are separated from the river by a dyke, and in spring the water level is topped up by the Danube floods. UNESCO listed the reserve in 1983, and it is also a Ramsar wetland and a biosphere reserve.

Birds are the reason. More than a hundred species breed in the reeds, and many others pass through on migration, since the Danube valley is a major flyway between Europe and Africa. The most famous resident is the Dalmatian pelican, one of the largest flying birds in the world, and Srebarna has one of the few breeding colonies in Europe. You may also see pygmy cormorants, glossy ibis, spoonbills, herons and great white egrets. In spring the air is filled with calls, and the sight of pelicans gliding in over the reeds is memorable.

The landscape is the Dobrudzha plain, an open, rolling country of wheat, sunflowers and maize that stretches to the Black Sea. Roads are straight and quiet, often lined with poplars, and the surface can be patchy. Heat in summer is considerable, and the wind can sweep across the plain. The best time to ride is spring or early autumn, when the fields are fresh or the sunflowers are in bloom, and the light is soft. Mornings are best for birds.

Silistra, a larger town on the Danube a short way east, is the place for fuel, food and rooms, while the villages near the lake have small shops and a few guesthouses. A visitor centre and a boardwalk give access to the reserve, and a small museum explains the ecology. Bring binoculars if you have them, and a hat for the sun. The ride connects with the Thracian tomb at Sveshtari and the Madara Rider, and you could make a rich day of it. Srebarna is a quiet place, and quiet is the whole idea.
t.southern battery no 3@60.0,29.7:
Sailors in the Gulf of Finland used to say that Kotlin Island was a long grey shape you saw only when you were already too close, and Southern Battery No. 3 is part of the reason the sailors came to respect it. It stands on the low, southern shore of the island, facing the channel that runs past Lomonosov on the mainland, one of a numbered line of coastal batteries that guarded the approach to Saint Petersburg from the sea. The batteries were built for guns and are now mostly quiet, grassy ruins of earth, brick and concrete.

The dam changed everything. Until the early twenty-first century the island was reachable only by water, which is why its fortifications stayed so well preserved, and then a long flood barrier was built across the gulf, with a road along the top. That road now links the island to the mainland on both sides, and a ride out here begins with a long, flat, windy run beside open water and the grey shapes of ships waiting for the port. In a strong westerly the bike will be pushed around, and in winter the surface can be glazed. The sea smells of salt and diesel.

On the island itself the roads are straight, flat and sometimes broken, and the area around the batteries is an odd mixture of military land, birch scrub and old earthworks. Some places are open to the public and some are not, so treat the coordinates as a general pointer and look for signs. Photography near active military sites can cause trouble, and it is worth asking before you point a camera at anything with a fence round it.

For fuel, rely on Kronstadt, which has over forty thousand people and a full range of shops. Cafes in the town are plain but warm, and the portions are generous. Lomonosov, on the mainland side, has a similar population and is the better place to stop if you are coming from the south.

The white nights of June make the long evening light on the water remarkable, and the island is quiet then. In autumn the weather turns fast, with fog and rain, and the long run on the dam can be unpleasant. Dress for the sea, not for the city.
t.southern battery no 1@60.0,29.7:
Kronstadt town has a face turned to the sea and a back turned to the mainland, and Southern Battery No. 1 stands on the southern shore of Kotlin Island, a few kilometres from the old harbour. It is one of the earth-and-brick gun batteries that formed part of the maritime fortress, built to protect the capital against any fleet that dared to enter the gulf. The island was fortified by Peter the Great, who founded the base here in the early eighteenth century, and it remained one of the great naval stations of the Russian empire.

The town has a long and sometimes violent history. The naval cathedral, with its huge dome, once dominated the skyline, and the great docks and basins still make up much of the waterfront. In 1921 the sailors of Kronstadt rose against the Bolshevik government, and the revolt was put down with great force, an event that still carries weight in the memory of the country. The old streets, with their neoclassical buildings and canals, have a faded grandeur, and a stroll through them is interesting.

Riding out to the battery involves a drive along the flood barrier, a long and exposed road across the water, with ships on one side and the open gulf on the other. The wind is often strong, and in winter the road can be icy. The roads on the island itself are flat and straight, with broken tarmac in places, and you may have to pick your way around potholes. The battery area is partly open, and signs will tell you where you may go.

Kronstadt has over forty thousand inhabitants and enough fuel stations, cafes and shops to meet a rider's needs. Lomonosov, on the mainland, is a similar size and is the alternative if you are approaching from the south.

The days around midsummer, when the light lingers almost until midnight, are the time to come. Spring and autumn bring fog and rain, and the winter is long and dark. The sea breeze brings a smell of salt and weed, and the cries of gulls are constant.
t.fort peter i@60.0,29.7:
Peter the Great wanted a fortress on the sea, and in the first years of the eighteenth century he got one, built on a sandbank and a few small islets in the shallows off Kotlin Island. Fort Peter I belongs to the chain of forts that grew from that first idea over the next two centuries, strung along the channels like beads on a thread, each with its own gun batteries, barracks and harbours. Together they formed a barrier that no enemy fleet cared to test, and during the Crimean War, when British and French ships came to the gulf, they thought better of attacking.

The forts stand in the open water, and the one on this ride is among those near the island's edge. Some are still military, some are abandoned and some are open to boat trips in summer. The coordinates mark the general area, and access depends on what is permitted at the time, so ask in Kronstadt or look for notices.

Kronstadt itself has a big presence on the island. It has over forty thousand people, with fuel stations and shops, and the old naval town is full of interest, from the great cathedral to the canals and docks. Lomonosov, on the mainland, with about forty-two thousand inhabitants, offers the same services and is a better place to start if you arrive from the south.

The ride here is mostly a matter of crossing the flood barrier, a long and windswept road, and then looking for a place to see the forts from the shore. The wind is the main hazard, and the surface of the road is rough in places. In winter the gulf freezes, and in the past people crossed the ice on foot or by sledge. Today the barrier road is open all year, though it is sometimes closed in severe storms.

White nights in June are a fine time to come. The water glows pink at midnight and the forts rise out of it like ships. In autumn the sea turns grey, the waves are short and steep, and the cold wind bites. A windproof jacket and a warm hat are essential, even in summer.
t.kronstadtskoe highway@60.0,29.7:
Anyone who rides to Kronstadt today does it along one of the strangest roads in Europe, a long causeway that crosses the Gulf of Finland on top of a flood barrier. The barrier was built to protect Saint Petersburg from storm surges, which have flooded the city many times since its founding, and the road runs along its top. On either side the water is open, grey and wide, with the cranes of the port and the low grey shapes of ships on the horizon. There is little to hold the wind, and a rider will feel every gust.

The highway lands on Kotlin Island, where the old naval town of Kronstadt sits at the eastern end. The road passes through flat land of scrub, old earthworks and battered brick, and on towards the town through a landscape that is more fortress than farm. The tarmac is mixed, with smooth stretches and rough, and traffic is light except at the start and end of the working day, when trucks and commuters fill the lanes.

The town has more than forty thousand people and offers fuel, shops and cafes in good supply. It was founded by Peter the Great as the base for his new Baltic fleet, and its buildings, canals and docks are among the best examples of imperial naval architecture in Russia. The great cathedral, with its huge dome, was built for the sailors and later used for other purposes, and has been restored in recent years.

Ride out in summer if you can. The evenings are long and the light on the water is strong, and the island is pleasant for a stroll. Autumn is wet and windy, and in winter the road can be treacherous with ice and snow. Fog can close in quickly, and visibility on the barrier may fall to a few hundred metres.

Check the weather and the traffic before you go, and keep a close eye on your fuel, since there are few places to stop on the barrier itself.
t.hogland@60.1,27.0:
Hogland, or Gogland to the Russians who now own it, is a lump of granite in the middle of the Gulf of Finland, a long boat ride from the Finnish coast near Kotka. There is no road to ride to it, so on a motorcycle route this point is a marker for the Gulf of Finland and the island itself rather than somewhere you will actually park. I mention it because the place has more history per square kilometre than anything else in these waters, and I would rather tell you honestly what I know than dress up a place I cannot take you to.

The island rises to a rocky ridge, the highest ground in the gulf, with pine on the slopes and a few small villages. Its fame comes from 1788, when a Russian fleet met a Swedish one in the Battle of Hogland, a bloody and inconclusive day that nonetheless wrecked Gustav III's plan to threaten St Petersburg by sea. The island belonged to Finland between the wars, with fishermen, a lighthouse and a Finnish-speaking population; in 1940, after the Winter War, it went to the Soviet Union and the Finns left. It is now a restricted border zone, so landing there is not a matter of simply turning up with a ferry ticket.

The gulf around it is shallow, cold and often foggy, and in winter it freezes, which the old pilots used as a road of its own. Seals and sea eagles use the skerries, and passing birds funnel along the coast in spring and autumn.

If you are riding the Finnish or Russian shore near here, fuel and food are in the towns on the coast; the nearest listed settlements are far enough away that the practical answer is to fill up in Kotka or Hamina on the Finnish side, or in the Leningrad region's coastal towns on the Russian side. Weather decides everything on this water, and the summer light lasts so long that you will find yourself looking at a white-grey horizon at eleven at night. Check current border and permit rules before planning anything near here, because they have changed repeatedly and are not something I would guess at.
t.northern battery no 6@60.0,29.9:
Kronstadt's guns were never only on the island. Peter the Great founded the fortress on Kotlin Island in 1703 to shut the mouth of the Neva, and over the next two centuries the defences spread across the shallows of the gulf, onto artificial islands and onto the northern shore, where numbered batteries covered the channel from the Karelian side. Northern Battery No. 6 belongs to that system, a low earthwork-and-masonry position on the coast near Gorskaya and Aleksandrovskaya, the old Gulf resort belt west of Lisy Nos. I would not describe its present condition, because many of these coastal works are overgrown, fenced off or partly demolished, and some are within restricted military land, so look from public roads and respect any barrier.

The coastal highway here is the gift. It is the old Primorskoye route, running in places beside the water, with pine woods and low dunes on one side and bay-side villas on the other, and it is perfect for a gentle evening ride. The surface is mostly decent. Traffic builds on summer weekends, when the dacha crowd heads for the beach. Strong onshore winds can come off the gulf, and in autumn the light is low and silver.

What makes this stretch interesting is the dam. The Saint Petersburg flood barrier, begun in 1979 and long delayed, runs from the northern shore through Kotlin Island to the southern shore, and carries the ring road, so the old fortress strategy has been replaced by a concrete answer to the surges that have flooded the city for three centuries. In 1824 the great flood reached terrible heights, the one Pushkin wrote about in The Bronze Horseman. Fields of reeds, low sand banks and flocks of ducks line the water here, and the shallow gulf is a stopover for migrating geese and swans.

Tarkhovka, about six kilometres off, is a modest town of around seven thousand people, and a better bet for a station than the two smaller villages. Fill the tank at the ring road or in Sestroretsk before going down the coast, and carry some cash and water. Cafes are scattered, mostly seasonal.
t.the barrier of cribwork@60.0,29.7:
Kronstadt is a naval town on an island, and nothing about it feels like anywhere else in Russia. Kotlin lies about thirty kilometres west of the centre of St Petersburg, a long thin island of some twelve kilometres, and when Peter's engineers decided to close the sea approaches in the early eighteenth century they did it with timber. The barrier of cribwork was a line of log cribs filled with stone, sunk across the shallow channels so that enemy ships could only pass under the guns, and this label points to that engineering memory rather than to anything you can ride up to and touch. The cribs rotted or were buried long ago, and the sea lanes are now marked by fort islands and the modern dam.

Today you reach Kronstadt by the ring road across the flood barrier, which has a tunnel-and-bridge section at the navigation gaps, and an entry checkpoint, so carry your passport and any registration papers, and check current rules before you plan the day. Kronstadt is a closed-style naval base with an open town, which is a strange mix. The streets are broad and straight, laid out on a Petrine grid, and the old port is quiet.

Look for the great naval cathedral, finished in 1913 with its pale dome that you can see from far out in the gulf, and for the Italian Palace, built for Prince Menshikov. The town was the base of the Baltic Fleet, the starting point of Russian polar and round-the-world expeditions, and in March 1921 it was the scene of a sailors' revolt against the Bolsheviks, crushed by troops who crossed the frozen gulf. Admiral Makarov, who pushed icebreaker design, is honoured by a monument.

Kronstadt has about forty-three thousand people, so fuel, cafes and shops are no trouble, and the town is flat and easy for a bike. The cobbles in the old quarter are rough, and wind off the water can be raw even in June. The best hour for a ride is the evening, when the low sun lights the fort silhouettes on the horizon and the fishermen on the quays are packing up their rods.
t.saynatsalo town hall@62.1,25.8:
Alvar Aalto won the competition for this building in 1949, and it was finished in 1952, a village council hall on a small island in Lake Päijänne that has become a pilgrimage for architects. Säynätsalo sits just across a short bridge from the town of Muurame, with Jyväskylä, the city where Aalto spent so much of his working life, a few kilometres north; the island is now part of Jyväskylä itself. The town hall is a cluster of red brick and timber around a raised courtyard of grass, and the council chamber stands over it with its high roof, fan-shaped wooden trusses and a hush of slanted light.

I find it the most human of Aalto's buildings, because he seems to have asked how a small community would want to meet. Brick was cheap and local, and he used it with a generous hand, letting ivy and moss climb over the courtyard walls. The ground-floor library and the mingled public rooms are still in use, and you can usually enter the courtyard and walk up the steps. Check summer opening times and guided tours before you go, as the interior access depends on the season and on whether the council chamber is in use.

The riding approach is one of Finland's best kinds of unremarkable. Roads curve through spruce and birch forests, past red barns and a succession of small lakes, with gentle grades and a few blind crests. Expect smooth tarmac but watch out for elk, especially at dusk, as they are both common and deadly. In summer the evening light never quite disappears, and Päijänne glitters in the long gold hours. Winter riding is not advisable.

Fuel and food are no problem. Muurame has nearly nine thousand people and the usual supermarkets and petrol stations, and Jyväskylä beyond it has everything. Finnish cafes serve a good cup of coffee with a cinnamon bun, and you will often find a lakeside spot to sit with a thermos. Take care with speed limits: Finnish fines are scaled to income, and cameras are common. Mosquitoes in June are fierce, so keep a jacket on near the water.
t.fort obrutchev@60.1,29.7:
Fort Obruchev stands on a man-made islet in the shallows of the Gulf of Finland, one of the chain of sea forts that gave Kronstadt its reputation as the strongest naval fortress in the world. Named, as I understand it, for General Nikolai Obruchev, a leading military planner of the late nineteenth century, it belongs to the northern line of the defences, built of granite and brick with casemates facing the main channel. Eight kilometres from Kronstadt town, it is reachable by boat or visible from the ring road across the dam, and in practice many of these forts are closed, derelict and under military control, so view it from a distance rather than expecting to land.

The great forts earned their fame in a war that never came. In 1854 and 1855, during the Crimean War, British and French ships entered the Baltic, and they decided that attacking Kronstadt was not worth the risk. The sea defences, combined with mines and shallow water, did their job simply by existing. The forts were rebuilt and modernised in the 1890s and again in the Soviet years, and they armed against a possible naval attack on Leningrad throughout the twentieth century. During the siege of Leningrad their guns supported the defence of the city, and their garrisons endured shelling and ice.

For a rider, the interest is in the road across the water. The dam highway runs for around twenty-five kilometres, and for long stretches you are riding with the open gulf on one side and the bay on the other, with ships far off and forts rising like grey rocks. It is windy, exposed, and often bitterly cold even in June, so wear a layer you do not need in the city. The surface is good and traffic moves fast, with trucks heading for the port.

Fuel is available in Kronstadt, eight kilometres off, or on the ring road at the mainland ends. Carry water and some food because the dam has no cafe stops, and remember that stopping on the carriageway is prohibited. In winter, with sea ice and snow, the view gets starker, and in clear weather on a September morning the gulf is the colour of pewter.
t.hudavendigar@40.2,29.0:
Bursa was the first capital of the Ottomans, and the Hüdavendigar Mosque in the hot-spring suburb of Çekirge is one of the earliest great buildings of the dynasty. Murad I, who conquered large parts of Thrace and the Balkans in the fourteenth century, took the title Hüdavendigâr, meaning sovereign, and the mosque complex that carries the name was built in the second half of that century. It has an unusual plan, with an upper floor that served as a school, and the shapes already show a style that would grow into the classical Ottoman mosque.

Çekirge has been known for its thermal baths since Roman times, and the water that flows from the slopes of Uludağ, the mountain behind the city, is still used in bathhouses that range from simple to ornate. A soak after a day on the road, in a marble hall with warm water running over the stone, is a fine way to end the day. In the city centre below, the Ulu Cami, the Great Mosque of 1399, has twenty domes and a fountain inside, and the Green Mosque and Green Tomb are famous for their blue-green tiles. The old market quarter near the Koza Han, a caravanserai once devoted to the silk trade, is the place to buy silk scarves and towels.

For riders, Bursa is a big, hilly city of more than a million, and traffic is heavy, with narrow streets near the old bazaars and steep slopes. The road up to Uludağ climbs through forest, with plenty of bends, to the ski resort at around 1,800 metres, and in summer it is a cool escape. Surfaces are generally good, although tram lines and cobbles in the old centre can be slippery in rain. Park the bike outside the market quarter and walk.

Fuel is easy everywhere. Bursa is also the home of İskender kebab, thin slices of lamb on bread with tomato sauce and melted butter, invented here in the nineteenth century, and candied chestnuts, kestane şekeri, are the local sweet. The peaches and the silk are famous too.

Spring, when the blossom is out and Uludağ still has snow on its summit, gives the best view.
t.burgas@42.5,27.5:
Burgas is the working heart of Bulgaria's southern Black Sea coast, a port city that has never quite decided whether it is industrial or seaside, and the answer is a little of both. The long Sea Garden, laid out in the late nineteenth century, runs along the cliff above the beach and is lined with statues, flowerbeds and cafes, and the pier at the end juts out into the bay like an invitation. The old railway station, with its fine early twentieth-century frontage, is a reminder of the city's role as a trading hub.

What sets Burgas apart is its lakes. Several shallow lagoons and salt pans lie right on the edge of the city, among them the Atanasovsko lake, whose pink salt pans glow in summer, and Vaya, the largest natural lake in Bulgaria. They lie on the Via Pontica, one of the main bird migration routes between Europe and Africa, and in spring and autumn tens of thousands of storks, pelicans, cranes and raptors pass through. If you ride out to the lakes in the early morning, you may see flamingos and avocets feeding in the shallows beside the road, a rather wonderful contrast to the chemical works in the background.

The best rides head along the coast. Heading north on the old road toward Pomorie, whose salt works and wine cellars are old traditions, you reach Nessebar, an ancient town on a rocky peninsula joined to the mainland by a narrow causeway. Its old town, with Byzantine churches and weathered wooden houses, is a World Heritage site, and it has been inhabited for more than three thousand years. South lies Sozopol, an equally old Greek colony, with narrow lanes of wooden houses above the water. The coastal roads are flat and curving, and can be busy with holidaymakers in July and August. Spring and autumn, with fewer people and mild weather, are better.

Fuel is easy in a city of nearly two hundred thousand, and the station network along the coast is dense. In Bulgaria, motorists and motorcyclists need an electronic vignette for the main roads, which is easy to buy online or at petrol stations, so check this before leaving. For food, look for fresh fried sprats, mussels, shopska salad and a glass of cold local white wine or rakia, and finish with a coffee in the shade.
t.varna@43.2,27.9:
Varna is Bulgaria's summer capital, a big, confident Black Sea city of three hundred thousand with a long beach, a grand seaside garden and a surprisingly deep past. In 1972, workers digging near the shore found a cemetery that has since become famous, the Varna Necropolis, which contained some of the oldest worked gold ever found, made around 4500 BC, long before the pharaohs. The treasures, which include tiny gold ornaments buried with the dead, are in the city's archaeological museum, and they show that a sophisticated society lived here thousands of years before Rome or Athens.

Varna was also a Greek colony, called Odessos, and later a Roman city, and the ruins of the Roman baths, among the largest in the Balkans, still stand near the centre. The Sea Garden, which runs for some kilometres along the cliff top, is a lovely place for a stroll, with old trees and a view of the bay, while the beaches below are crowded in summer. Eat well here: fresh fish, mussels, tarator, the cold cucumber and yoghurt soup, and a plate of grilled vegetables with local cheese make a good lunch.

For riders, the city is a fine base for a day trip inland to Madara, about ninety kilometres to the west, near Shumen. There, high on a sheer cliff above the village, is the Madara Rider, a large relief carved into the rock in the early eighth century, showing a horseman spearing a lion while a dog runs behind him. It is the only such monument of its kind in Europe and is a World Heritage site. The road there passes through low green hills, farmland and sunflower fields, with long straights and gentle curves, and the steps up the cliff lead to a view across the plain. Summer is hot, and a morning start is a good idea.

Closer to town, the Aladzha Monastery, a medieval rock-cut complex in the forest north of the city, is a quiet place for an hour. The streets of Varna itself can be hectic, so ride with alertness and allow time for traffic in the centre. Fuel is available throughout the city and the main roads, and nearby Asparuhovo and Aksakovo have several stations. Remember the electronic vignette that is needed in Bulgaria, and carry some cash for parking and small cafes in the villages.
t.san cristobal de las casas@16.7,-92.6:
San Cristóbal de las Casas sits at about 2,200 metres in a bowl of pine and oak forest in the Chiapas highlands, and the altitude shapes everything. The mornings are cold, the afternoons bright and the evenings smoky with wood fires, and the old streets, cobbled and low, are lined with houses painted in ochre and red. Diego de Mazariegos founded the town in 1528, and it was later renamed for Bartolomé de las Casas, the Dominican bishop who spoke up for the Indigenous population. On New Year's Day 1994 the Zapatista rebels briefly took over the town hall, and the uprising still shapes the politics of the region.

The ride up from the lowlands is the real attraction, with a long climb through forest and a succession of tight bends, and signs for villages whose names are in Tzotzil and Tzeltal. Be ready for the topes, the speed bumps that guard every settlement and can be vicious at the wrong speed. Fog and drizzle are common in the rainy season from May to October, and the road can be slick, so ride within what you can see. Dry season from November to April gives clearer skies, though nights are cold enough for a proper jacket.

Walk the centre, which is pedestrian-friendly, and visit the Santo Domingo church with its elaborate baroque front and the markets next to it, where Maya weavers sell textiles. Chiapas is also known for amber, which comes from local mines and is sold in small shops. A short ride away, the village of San Juan Chamula has a church where the rituals blend Catholic and older Maya traditions, and photography inside is strictly forbidden, so respect that. Zinacantán, nearby, is known for flowers and weaving.

The city has Pemex stations around the edges, plenty of cafes serving local coffee and a surprising number of good restaurants. Park the bike somewhere secure overnight, since the centre is dense with tourists and the streets are narrow. The altitude can make you a little breathless on the first day, so go gently, drink water and take your time.
t.springfield missouri@37.2,-93.3:
Springfield, Missouri, calls itself the birthplace of Route 66, and the claim has a document behind it. On 30 April 1926 officials from Springfield sent a telegram proposing that the new highway from Chicago to Los Angeles be numbered 66, and the idea was accepted. The city of about a hundred and sixty-seven thousand grew up around the railroads and the highway, and many of the old motels and diners from the golden age still stand along St. Louis Street and College Street, with their neon signs and mid-century lines.

History here goes well beyond the road. On the town square in 1865, Wild Bill Hickok shot Davis Tutt in a face-to-face gunfight, widely regarded as the first true quick-draw duel of the Old West. A few miles south-west, the battlefield at Wilson's Creek preserves the site of the first major Civil War battle fought west of the Mississippi, in August 1861, where the Union general Nathaniel Lyon was killed. The Ozarks, the old wooded hills on which Springfield stands, are known for their caves, springs and rivers.

The city is also the home of Bass Pro Shops, the vast outdoor-goods chain, and of a rather peculiar local dish, Springfield-style cashew chicken, invented in the 1960s by a Chinese-American restaurateur and now served in restaurants all over town. It is deep-fried, drowned in brown sauce and sprinkled with cashews, and it is surprisingly good.

As a place to start a ride on Route 66, Springfield is easy. The old road heads west through Missouri farmland and small towns, with gentle rolling hills, and the surface is a mix of original concrete, patched tarmac and modern road. Speed limits are low, and the pace is meant to be slow. Fuel is available everywhere, with large stations at every junction, and you can eat and sleep to any budget. Summer is hot and humid, with thunderstorms that can roll in fast, and winter ice can close the roads, so spring and autumn are the best seasons. At dusk, the neon signs glow, and the old road feels briefly alive.
t.galena kansas@37.1,-94.6:
Galena, Kansas, is the first or last town on the shortest stretch of Route 66 in any state, just thirteen miles in the south-east corner of Kansas, and the town makes the most of it. The name is Latin for lead ore, and the place was founded in the 1870s when miners struck rich lead and zinc deposits in the Tri-State District, which spread across Kansas, Missouri and Oklahoma. The boom made it a rowdy town of thousands, and the legacy remains in the huge piles of mine waste, known as chat, which still stand on the horizon, and in the contaminated ground that has taken decades to clean up.

Today Galena is a quiet town of fewer than three thousand people, and its best-known attraction is a restored old filling station on the main road, now a cafe and souvenir shop called Cars on the Route. The tow truck parked outside, a rusting old International, was one of the inspirations for Mater in the Pixar film Cars, and the whole place has the cheerful, slightly worn charm of Route 66 at its best. The old route is signposted, and a few other relics, including a small mining museum, are worth a stop.

Between Galena and Baxter Springs the old road crosses the Rainbow Bridge, a concrete arch bridge of a rare type, built in 1923. Baxter Springs has its own history, with a Civil War massacre in 1863 and a bank robbery attributed to Jesse James, and a small heritage centre tells the story.

The riding is a pleasant, easy cruise, with a gentle landscape of rolling prairie and small farms, and the old road is narrow, with patches of ageing concrete. Traffic is light, and the pace is slow. Fuel is available in Galena and Baxter Springs, and both have diners and cafes. Summer is hot and humid, with storms and occasional tornado warnings, so the best months are spring and autumn. Stop at a roadside cafe and talk to the locals, who are proud of their short stretch of the road.
t.gabrovo@42.9,25.3:
Gabrovo is the town where the Balkan Mountains begin to rise in earnest, strung along the narrow valley of the Yantra River in central Bulgaria, and it is best known for a joke. The town has a reputation, among Bulgarians, for thrift, and the legends of its stinginess have produced a whole genre of humour. The House of Humour and Satire, a museum devoted to it, is one of the stranger attractions in the country, and the town holds a biennial carnival of humour. Locals take the whole thing with good grace, and a visitor who tells a thrift joke will probably be rewarded with a better one.

Behind the jokes lies a history of industry. Gabrovo was an early centre of textile manufacturing in the Ottoman era and the first Bulgarian town to have a secular school, and its craftsmen and merchants were prominent in the national revival of the nineteenth century. A few kilometres to the south, the Etar Architectural-Ethnographic Complex is an open-air museum where craftsmen work in water-powered workshops and demonstrate traditional crafts in a collection of old houses.

For riders, Gabrovo is the doorway to the Shipka Pass, one of the best-known mountain roads in Bulgaria. The road climbs south from town through beech forest, crosses the main ridge of the Balkan at about 1,185 metres, and descends into the Valley of the Roses near Kazanlak, with plenty of bends and a surface that is generally good. At the top, a huge stone monument stands on Stoletov Peak, commemorating the fierce battles of 1877 and 1878, when Russian and Bulgarian volunteers held the pass against Ottoman forces in the war that led to Bulgaria's liberation. A steep staircase leads to the memorial, and the view over the mountains is wide. The pass can be icy or snowy in winter, and fog sometimes sits in the beech forest, so check conditions before you go.

Gabrovo has more than sixty thousand people, so fuel, food and accommodation are no problem. Tryavna, thirteen kilometres to the south-west, is a lovely old town of wooden houses and cobbled lanes that deserves an hour, and the road toward it is fun.

Try a bowl of shopska salad and some grilled meat in a mehana, a traditional tavern, and finish with Bulgarian rakia.
t.mikkeli@61.7,27.3:
Finland's Lakeland does not rise, it spreads. Mikkeli lies in the middle of the Saimaa region, in the province of South Savo, on a landscape of long glacial ridges, forest and water that stretches in every direction. The town has about forty-six thousand people, which makes it the biggest place for a long way, and its centre sits on the shore of Lake Saimaa with a small harbour and a market square where you can buy fresh vendace, the little fish called muikku, fried crisp and eaten with mashed potato.

The history is more serious than the setting suggests. During the Second World War, Mikkeli was the headquarters of the Finnish armed forces, and Marshal Mannerheim directed the war from here through the Winter War and the Continuation War. The headquarters building is now a museum, and the whole district keeps a quiet pride in that role. A short climb up the hill of Naisvuori brings you to an observation tower with a view over the town and the lake, which in midsummer remains lit until very late at night, since the sun barely sets this far north.

The roads here are a very different pleasure from the Alps or the Mediterranean. Highway 62 and the minor roads that thread between the lakes are smooth, quiet, and shaded by pine and birch, with long, relaxed curves and the occasional causeway or bridge across a narrow strait. Speed limits are strictly enforced and cameras are common, so ride accordingly. The main hazard is wildlife: elk, which Finns call moose, can step out at dusk, and the sudden appearance of a thousand kilos of animal on a quiet road is a risk worth respecting.

Saimaa is also home to one of the rarest seals in the world, the Saimaa ringed seal, which lives only in these lakes and survives in small numbers. You are unlikely to spot one from the road, but it is a reminder of how particular this landscape is. The water is clear and brown-tinted from the peat, and the smell of pine resin and damp earth after rain lingers everywhere.

Mikkeli has all the services you need, including fuel at several stations, supermarkets and cafes, and the summer season from June to August is easily the best for riding, with warm days and endless light.
