t.puumala@61.5,28.2:
Puumala sits on a narrow strait in the middle of Lake Saimaa, the biggest lake in Finland, and the whole village is arranged around the point where road and water meet. Saimaa is less a single lake than an endless puzzle of channels, bays and islands, thousands of them, and the road here crosses the water on a bridge over the Puumalansalmi strait, with the glittering lake on either side and a light shimmering off the surface in summer. The endangered Saimaa ringed seal, which lives nowhere else in the world, swims in these waters, though you will be very lucky to catch a glimpse of one.

There is a small curiosity in the name. Puumala gave its name to a virus, the Puumala hantavirus, first identified in bank voles in this area, and an odd bit of scientific fame for a village of about twenty-seven hundred people. Mostly it is a place for summer cottages, boating and fishing, with a harbour, a few shops and a church. Savonlinna and Mikkeli are the larger towns around the lake, each an hour or so away, with Savonlinna's medieval castle of Olavinlinna, built in the fifteenth century, being the best known.

The riding is the reward. The Saimaa Road 62 follows lake shores and crosses straits through forests of pine and birch, with gentle curves, fast stretches and long views, and the traffic is light. Speed limits are strict and fines in Finland are linked to income, so keep within them. The real hazards are elk and deer at dawn and dusk, and the occasional gravel at junctions. Summer evenings are long and light, and in June it hardly gets dark. September gives crisp air and colours.

Practicalities are easy enough. A village of this size has at least a petrol station and a supermarket, though hours can be short on Sundays, and the café culture is better than you might expect, with coffee and a cinnamon bun, korvapuusti, on almost every counter. Look for fresh vendace, a small lake fish, fried in butter, a Saimaa classic, usually served at harbour kiosks in summer. Take a swim off a jetty if the weather allows, since the water is clean and soft and surprisingly bearable in late July.
t.jyvaskyla@62.2,25.8:
Jyväskylä rises from the shore of a lake in the middle of Finland's lakeland, a student town of about eighty-five thousand people with a surprisingly big architectural reputation. The great Finnish architect Alvar Aalto grew up and studied in the region and left his mark all over the place: the university campus, the museum devoted to his work, the Workers' Club and the little town hall in Säynätsalo, on an island in the lake a few kilometres to the south, are all his. Even if you know nothing of architecture, the red brick, the long windows and the way the buildings fit into the woodland make an impression. It is that kind of town, quietly proud of its design.

The country around is a wide patchwork of lakes and low forested ridges, shaped by the last ice age. Long, narrow ridges called eskers run between the lakes, and in several places roads follow their crests, so you ride with water glinting on both sides. Birch and pine fill the slopes, the air smells of resin, and in autumn the colours are superb. Jyväskylä is also the home of Finland's round of the World Rally Championship, and during the event in summer the forest roads are thrilling to watch. For motorcyclists this means the roads are well maintained, wide and fast, with fine surfaces.

Out of the city, the day's riding tends to be gentle: broad, easy curves, little traffic and the occasional dip down to a lake shore. Speed limits are strictly enforced, with automatic cameras on many main roads, so watch the signs, and keep an eye out for elk at dusk. Fuel is no problem. The city and its neighbours Muurame and Säynätsalo have petrol stations, supermarkets and cafés, and bakeries sell fresh cinnamon buns by the dozen.

Evenings are the best time. In June and July the light lasts until midnight, and the lakes turn silver and then pink. It is a good place to finish a day, with a sauna to go with it, as nearly every Finn will tell you.
t.ozark@35.5,-93.8:
Ozark, Arkansas, sits on the south side of the Arkansas River valley, where the flat bottomlands end and the Ozark foothills begin. It is a quiet county seat of about thirty-five hundred people, with an old courthouse on a square, a few brick storefronts and a couple of cafes, and it serves as the starting point for the Pig Trail, the road that heads north through the Ozark National Forest toward Eureka Springs and Fayetteville. The name itself may come from the French aux Arcs, to the Arkansas, though the exact origin is debated.

The river valley here is farm country, with fields of hay and cattle on the flat land, but the country to the north changes quickly. The Boston Mountains, the highest part of the Ozarks, rise steeply with tight hollows, hardwood forests of oak and hickory, and clear creeks. Arkansas Highway 23, the Pig Trail, got its nickname from the students and fans of the University of Arkansas Razorbacks, who used the road to drive to football games at Fayetteville. The state has since designated it a scenic byway, and it is widely considered one of the best motorcycle roads in the South.

The road is a real challenge: dozens of tight curves and switchbacks, with steep climbs and descents, and a surface that is generally good but can be gritty in places. Traffic is light on weekdays, and weekends bring hordes of riders, especially in October. Spring brings dogwood and redbud, summer green and heat, and autumn a blaze of color. The Mulberry River, a popular canoeing stream, runs nearby, and the little community of Cass offers a place for a break. Watch for gravel on bends, and take care when the leaves fall and the road is slippery.

Ozark has fuel, a supermarket and several restaurants, which makes it a handy start. There are fewer services on the Pig Trail, so fill up before heading north. The town of Mulberry, a short ride west, offers more options. The best months are April, May and mid-October, when the weather is mild and the scenery at its peak, but summer afternoons can be hot and humid, with thunderstorms that arrive quickly. Deer are a constant danger, especially at dawn and dusk, and even in daylight they cross the road without warning.
t.jasper@36.0,-93.2:
Jasper is a tiny town in the heart of the Arkansas Ozarks, with a courthouse square, a few shops and a population under five hundred, but it sits at the junction of some of the best scenery in the region. The Buffalo National River, the first river in the United States to be protected as a national river, flows nearby in a long, winding course between limestone bluffs, and Jasper is one of the gateways to it. The surroundings are steep, forested hills, with deep hollows, creeks and rock outcrops.

The Buffalo is a clear green stream that runs for about a hundred and fifty miles, mostly free of dams, and its bluffs are some of the tallest in the Ozarks, with cliffs of pale limestone that drop straight to the water. In autumn and winter the valley around Boxley, a short ride north, is home to a herd of elk, reintroduced in the 1980s after the animals had vanished from Arkansas a century earlier, and in September and October the bulls bugle in the meadows at dawn. Whitaker Point, a rock ledge above a deep canyon, is one of the most photographed spots in the state, though it requires a hike.

The road is the big draw. Arkansas Highway 7, a scenic byway, runs through Jasper in a series of curves and climbs, along ridgelines and down into valleys, with long views over layered hills. The stretch south of town, down toward the Buffalo River valley, is especially good, with hairpins and steep grades. The surface varies from good to rough, and traffic can be heavy on autumn weekends. Weather is mild in spring and fall, hot and humid in summer, with occasional heavy rain that can wash gravel across the road.

Services in Jasper are limited but real: a station, a store and a few small restaurants, while Harrison, about twenty-six kilometers north, has the big supermarkets and motels. It is wise to fill the tank in Harrison or here before heading deeper into the hills. The best times are April for dogwood and redbud, and October for color. Deer, and sometimes elk, can wander onto the road at dusk, and the dense forest makes visibility short on the curves.
t.joensuu@62.6,29.8:
Joensuu sits on the Pielisjoki River in North Karelia, close to the Russian border in eastern Finland, and it was planned from scratch. Tsar Nicholas I founded the town in 1848, and its streets are laid out in a neat grid around a central square, with a graceful town hall and a wide river promenade. It is the capital of Finnish Karelia, a region of forest and lakes, and a university town with a youthful feeling, in spite of its distance from the capital.

Joensuu calls itself the forest capital of Finland, with forestry research institutes and a long relationship with the timber industry. The region of North Karelia is also known for its food: karjalanpiirakka, the Karelian pie, a thin rye crust filled with rice and topped with egg butter, is the regional specialty, along with fish dishes and berry desserts. Finland's eastern border region has a complicated history, as much of historic Karelia was lost to the Soviet Union in the Second World War, and many Karelian evacuees resettled around Joensuu.

For riders, the countryside north and east of town offers long, quiet roads through endless forest and lakes. Roads run toward Koli, a national park on a ridge above Lake Pielinen, whose rounded hilltops give the most famous views in Finland, with a huge panorama of water and forest. The road surface is good, speeds are limited and enforced with cameras, and traffic is light. The landscape is mostly flat to gently rolling, with the forest of spruce, pine and birch broken by lakes.

Joensuu has fuel, supermarkets, restaurants and hotels, and it is the last big town before the wilderness, so top up. The best months are June to August, with bright nights and warm days, and September, with autumn colors known as ruska, which are at their best here. Winter is long and cold, with snow and ice, making riding impractical. Reindeer and elk can wander onto the road, particularly in the north, and mosquitoes are fierce in summer, so carry repellent for the stops.
t.kajaani@64.2,27.7:
Kajaani is a quiet town in central Finland, in the region of Kainuu, but its quiet is deceptive, because in this modest place a good part of Finnish culture was written down. In the 1830s the physician Elias Lönnrot worked here as a district doctor and traveled through the surrounding villages, collecting oral poetry from singers, and from those verses he compiled the Kalevala, the national epic of Finland, first published in 1835. A statue and a small museum in town recall his work.

The town sits on the Kajaani River, between two lakes, and the ruins of a castle, built by the Swedes in the early seventeenth century and destroyed by the Russians in the Great Northern War, still stand by the rapids. The central streets are laid out wide, and a neat town hall and wooden church stand among them. Industry has long included timber and paper, and the region has a strong tradition of rural life.

For riders, the lure is the road north and east. The Raate Road, near the Russian border, was the site of a famous battle in the Winter War of 1939 and 1940, when Finnish troops destroyed Soviet divisions in the forest, and a memorial marks the site. Hossa, farther north, has rock paintings thousands of years old on a lake cliff, and a national park of pine forest. The roads there are long, nearly straight and empty, running through endless forest, with marshes, lakes and the occasional village. Road surfaces are good, but the distances are large, and services are sparse.

Kajaani has fuel, supermarkets and hotels, and it is the place to fill up and eat before heading north. The best months are June to August, with the light lasting almost all night in midsummer, and September, when the colors are spectacular. Winter is long, cold and dark. Reindeer, elk and bears roam the wilderness, and collisions with elk are a genuine risk, so keep speed down and watch the verges. Mosquitoes and midges are intense in July, so bring repellent.
t.oberon high country@-33.7,149.9:
The high country around Oberon sits on the plateau west of the Blue Mountains, a cool tableland more than a thousand metres above sea level, where the air is clean and the winters are properly cold. Oberon itself is a town of about three thousand people, surrounded by farms, pine plantations and the forests of Kanangra-Boyd and Jenolan State Forest. The surrounding country is a rolling grassland, with granite outcrops, sheep and cattle, and stands of snow gum and peppermint, quite unlike the sandstone and eucalyptus of the mountains to the east.

Oberon's story is largely one of timber. The big softwood plantations established here in the twentieth century made it a centre of the industry, and the sawmills and timber trucks are an important part of local life. The town is also known for its frosts and occasional snowfalls, which are uncommon in most of New South Wales. In winter, a dusting of snow draws visitors from Sydney, and the roads may be icy in the early morning.

Riding in the high country is a pleasure, with long, flowing roads across the tableland, and fewer cars than on the roads of the Blue Mountains. The corners are broad and the surfaces generally good, though verges are soft, and logging trucks use many of the roads, so keep to the left and give them space. The road to Jenolan Caves descends into a deep limestone valley by way of a series of tight bends, and is a classic ride. The caves, among the oldest open caves in the world, were known to the Gundungurra people long before Europeans arrived, and guided tours go down into the cathedral-like chambers. The final approach, through a rock tunnel known as the Grand Arch, is dramatic.

Weather here is changeable. Summers are mild and sometimes hot, and autumn brings beautiful colours in the plantings of exotic trees. Winters are cold, with frosts and fog. Kangaroos and wallabies are common at dusk, and wombats may be seen on the roads at night.

Oberon is large enough to have fuel, supermarkets, bakeries and pubs, which makes it the sensible stop on the plateau. Lithgow, thirty-six kilometres to the north-east, is the next big town. Fill up in Oberon before heading into the forests, and carry a warm layer even on a summer day.
t.tuxtla gutierrez@16.8,-93.1:
Tuxtla Gutiérrez is the capital of Chiapas, a big, hot, busy city in a valley at about 520 metres, and it is not the most beautiful place in southern Mexico but it is very useful. With around half a million people, it has everything from fuel to repair shops to big supermarkets, and it is the sensible place to start a ride into the highlands. The name comes from the Nahuatl for the place of rabbits, and the city's symbol is a rabbit. The Zoológico Miguel Álvarez del Toro, a zoo that focuses on the animals of Chiapas, is one of the best in Mexico and is set in a hillside forest.

The real attraction is the Sumidero Canyon, a deep gorge whose walls rise over a thousand metres above the Grijalva river. A road leads to several viewpoints at the rim, and boats run along the river at the bottom, where crocodiles bask on the banks and herons stand in the shallows. The canyon was formed by a crack in the earth's crust and later by the river, and it is spectacular in morning light. Riders can reach the viewpoints on a short, winding road from the city.

Leaving town, the route climbs toward San Cristóbal de las Casas, at over 2,100 metres, through pine forests and mountain villages. The road is a main highway, with curves, long climbs and mist, and the surface is generally decent. Trucks and buses crawl on the uphill sections, and passing requires patience. Be alert for topes, the speed bumps found in every village, and for stray livestock. In the rainy season, from May to October, fog and heavy rain are common in the highlands.

Food in Chiapas is distinct: try cochito, a pork dish, sopa de pan, and the local coffee, which is some of the best in the country. Chiapas is also home to many Maya communities, and their textiles and traditions are visible in the markets. Fill the tank in Tuxtla before the climb, take cash, and consider starting early, since the heat in the valley builds fast. By the time you reach the cool pines, the city feels far away.
t.sumidero canyon@16.9,-93.1:
The Sumidero Canyon is a crack in the Chiapas highlands with the Grijalva river at the bottom, and its walls run up to about a kilometre in places. Most visitors see it from a boat that leaves Chiapa de Corzo, but a rider gets the other view, from the rim road that climbs out of Tuxtla and visits a string of lookouts along the edge. Each has its own name, its own car park and its own stall selling fruit and sweets, and each shows the same trench from a different angle: vertical rock, green water, and a ribbon of foam far below. The water is a lake now, held back by the Chicoasén dam, finished in 1980, so the canyon is a flooded canyon, though it is no less dramatic for that.

The riding to get to it is short and simple. The road leaves Tuxtla, the state capital, and rises through dry forest and farmland to the national park gate, with a decent surface, wide bends and ample room for a rider to look about. Traffic is light on weekdays. At the miradores the ground is rough and the edges are often barely fenced, so watch your feet, and keep your helmet on when you walk to the rail. The heat is heavy by late morning, and the haze can wash out the photographs, so the first hours of the day serve you best.

There is a story people tell here, though how much of it is history and how much memory is hard to say. When the Spaniards came in the 1520s, the Chiapa warriors are said to have chosen to throw themselves into the gorge rather than surrender, and the canyon has carried that dark pride ever since. Crocodiles still sun themselves on the banks, spider monkeys cross the canopy, and vultures ride the thermals at eye level from the lookouts.

Fuel and food are easy in Tuxtla, a city of half a million, twelve kilometres from the park gate, so fill up before you climb. At the rim you will find cheap snacks, fresh fruit with chilli and lime, and drinks. Bring your own water all the same, because the sun is fierce, and there is little shade at most of the lookouts.
t.comitan@16.3,-92.1:
Comitán sits at around 1,600 metres in the highlands of eastern Chiapas, closer to Guatemala than to any large Mexican city, and it has the slightly reserved, self-contained air of a town that has been far from things for a long time. Its full name honours Belisario Domínguez, the local doctor and senator who stood up in the Senate in 1913 and denounced the dictator Victoriano Huerta, and was murdered for it. His statue, his museum, and the main square named for him tell visitors how the town sees itself. Another famous daughter is the writer Rosario Castellanos, whose novels and poems of Chiapas are still read widely.

The ride in is a pleasure after the long grind along the Pan-American Highway. The country is pine-oak forest, cattle pasture and farm plots in a rolling landscape, cool in the mornings, with mist in the folds of the valleys. The road bends gently with good views, but there are topes, the speed bumps of Mexico, at every village, so ease off at the sign. Trucks are slow on the climbs and the highway shoulders are narrow, so overtake with patience. In the rainy season, from May to October, afternoon downpours are heavy.

The town itself is a handsome place of low colonial houses, a big arcaded plaza and a church, and it is lively in the evening when families fill the squares. The local drink is comiteco, a spirit distilled from agave in the same family as tequila and mezcal, drunk in small glasses and proudly claimed as theirs. Posol, a cold maize drink often sold in the market, is the traditional refresher, and the food is Chiapan, with tamales, black beans, and grilled meats. Look for the stalls selling cheese and bread, which are hard to beat.

Comitán has about a hundred thousand people, so fuel, banks, repair shops and hotels are plentiful. It is also the gateway to the Lagos de Montebello, a group of lakes in pine forest about an hour away, in many shades of blue and green, and to the Lacandon forest beyond. Cool nights surprise visitors who think of southern Mexico as hot, so keep a layer in the bag. If you can spare the time, stay overnight and ride out in the morning light.
t.montebello lakes@16.1,-91.7:
The Lagunas de Montebello is a cluster of around sixty lakes scattered through pine forest on the border with Guatemala, and they come in colours that look improbable. Some are turquoise, some deep green, some blue-grey, and the shades change with the light and the minerals in the water. The lakes sit in a limestone karst landscape at about 1,500 metres, where underground rivers and sinkholes feed them, and the park is a protected national area. The small villages around, such as Tziscao, Miguel Hidalgo and Ojo de Agua, are home to Tojolabal and Mam communities and a few families who run cabins and food stalls.

The ride from Comitán de Domínguez is easy and pleasant, with a road that climbs through cool pine and oak forest, with mist in the mornings. Surface quality is fair, but topes and potholes are common, and local trucks and pickups are slow. The air is crisp, and the quiet is notable after the traffic of the plateau. This is a region of strong Maya heritage, and the border with Guatemala, a few kilometres away, is not a fence but a line through the forest.

Some of the lakes are named, such as Tziscao, with a beach and boats, and Laguna Bosque Azul, and the Cinco Lagos, a group with different shades. At Tziscao, you can walk to the border marker. The water is cold, but swimming is allowed in some lakes. Birds are abundant, and in the forest, you may see quetzals, though that is a matter of luck and patience.

Simple food is available from stalls and small restaurants, with quesadillas, tamales and fresh trout, plus coffee grown nearby. The dry season, November to April, is best, as the rainy months can bring heavy showers. Bring a warm layer, because the air at altitude is cooler than you expect, and the water is a fine reward.
t.winslow@35.8,-94.1:
Winslow, Arkansas, is a small place on a big hill. It sits at around 520 metres in the Boston Mountains, the highest part of the Ozarks, on US 71, which for generations was the main road between Fort Smith and Fayetteville, and the old highway still twists up through the town in a series of bends that every trucker once cursed. The town has fewer than five hundred people and a handful of shops and cafes, but its position makes it a natural place to pause between the valley and the high country.

The geography is the story. The Boston Mountains are not really mountains, but a deeply dissected plateau of sandstone and shale, cut by creeks into narrow valleys and steep ridges, with a thick cover of oak and hickory that blazes in October. Roads here follow the ridge crests wherever they can and plunge into hollows where they cannot, and that makes the riding excellent. The curves are tight and frequent, the gradients steady and the surface variable, with some good, some patched. Weekday traffic is light, but weekends, especially in autumn, bring more cars. Watch for deer, gravel on corners, and the odd log truck.

Winslow's history is tied to the railway, which crossed the divide here in a tunnel in the 1880s, and the town developed around the line. The old highway and the railway have shaped the community, which still has some tidy older buildings and a few reminders of the days when travellers stopped for the night. In summer, the cool air at altitude made it a minor resort for visitors escaping the heat of the lowlands.

Winslow itself has a couple of small stores and eating places, and petrol may be available, though I would not rely on hours. The reliable options are West Fork, about fifteen kilometres to the north, and Prairie Grove to the north-west, which has more shops. Fayetteville, bigger still, lies beyond. For a longer day, a stop for pie at a local cafe is the traditional answer. Keep an eye on the weather, since fog can settle on the ridge and spring storms can be violent.
t.devils den@35.8,-94.2:
Devils Den is a state park in a cleft of the Boston Mountains, and the name comes from the rock itself: a tangle of crevices, caves and fractured sandstone ledges, where the ground opens in narrow corridors that you can squeeze through, with moss on the walls and ferns in the cracks. It is a lovely, slightly gloomy place on a wet day, and in summer the cool air flowing out of the crevices is a relief. Lee Creek runs through the valley below, clear and quick over sandstone ledges.

The park was developed in the 1930s by the Civilian Conservation Corps, young men who built the stone cabins, the dam that forms a small lake, and the trails, using local sandstone. Their work is still in use today, and it gives the park a handsome, old-fashioned look, with solid rock walls and rustic buildings that fit the landscape. A visitor centre explains the history, and the old CCC buildings are well kept. Some of the trails lead past rock shelters that were used for centuries by Native people.

Reaching the park is part of the fun. Highway 170, the road from West Fork, is a narrow, twisting route down through the hardwood forest, with sharp bends, steep sections and a rough surface in places. It is a favourite of Arkansas motorcyclists, and at weekends you will see groups of bikes parked by the entrance. The surrounding Boston Mountains Scenic Loop uses a series of back roads that climb, drop and wander, and the best time is autumn, when the maples and hickories turn, or spring, when dogwood and redbud flower. The roads can be slick with wet leaves and mud, and the sudden rain showers come quickly.

The park has a campground, cabins and a small restaurant, but not much else. West Fork, about seventeen kilometres away, has petrol and a few shops, and Prairie Grove and Fayetteville have more. Fill up before you head into the hills, since the roads are long and the signs few. Wear boots if you plan to walk, because the rocks are slick, and be aware that the crevices are best explored in daylight, with a torch.
t.clarksville arkansas@35.5,-93.5:
Clarksville sits in the Arkansas River Valley, in the low country between the Boston Mountains to the north and the long, flat-topped ridge of Mount Magazine to the south. It is a proper small city of nine thousand or so, with a courthouse square, a college, a ring of motels along the interstate, and a reputation that rests on one fruit: Johnson County peaches. In summer the roadside stands sell them by the bushel, and the local festival has been running for decades. If you pass through in July, eat one and judge for yourself.

The town is also a staging post. University of the Ozarks sits on a hill above the centre, and the interstate runs along the valley floor, making this a convenient place to find fuel, food, and a bed. The restaurants run to catfish, burgers, and plate lunches, and the coffee is serviceable. This is the practical beginning of the ride, and you should use it that way: fill the tank, eat a proper breakfast, and buy water, because the climb north takes you into forest where services thin out fast.

From here, the route heads north on state highway 21 into the Ozark National Forest. Within a few kilometres, the road starts to rise and curl, and the farms give way to oak and hickory woodland. The Boston Mountains are the highest part of the Ozarks, a rugged plateau cut into steep hollows rather than true peaks, which means the road keeps climbing and dropping through folds in the land. The corners are tight enough to be fun, the surface is generally decent, and the traffic is light on a weekday. Watch for gravel on corners, and for deer at dusk, which are plentiful here.

Spring brings dogwood and redbud in the understory, and October turns the hardwoods into some of the best autumn colour in the middle of the country. Summer is hot and humid, with thunderstorms building in the afternoon, so ride early. Winter ice can close the higher sections of road for a day or two.

If you have a spare hour, Mount Magazine, the highest point in Arkansas, is reachable to the south, and has an excellent view over the valley. But the main attraction is north, and Clarksville is the place to set off from.
t.oark@35.7,-93.6:
Oark is a place that exists mostly because motorcyclists love it. A handful of buildings stand at a crossroads in the Ozark National Forest, and the general store is the centre of everything. On a good weekend there are dozens of bikes parked outside, and riders from three or four states are comparing notes on the roads they have just ridden. Highways 21, 215, and 103 meet here, and all three are good, which is why people come.

The land is hill country, steep and densely forested, with creeks running through hollows and sandstone bluffs showing through the oaks and hickories. The Ozark Highlands Scenic Byway threads through the middle of it, and the roads are some of the best in the central United States for a rider who likes endless curves. The corners are mostly open and well-surfaced, though the hills hide tighter bends and the occasional damp patch under trees. Leaves fall thick in autumn and can make the road slippery, so ride the colours with a gentle hand.

The store is a genuine old general store, and it has the feel of one: wooden floors, shelves of odd goods, and a lunch counter that serves burgers and pies to a hungry crowd. It is the kind of place where the food is good because people have been coming for it for a long time, not because anyone decided to make it so. Expect a wait on busy weekends, and expect to enjoy it. There is nothing much else here, apart from a few houses and the road itself.

Do not expect fuel in Oark. Clarksville, about twenty-six kilometres south, is the nearest bigger town with stations and supplies, and it is wise to fill up there before heading up into the hills. Coal Hill and other small towns are farther off. Spring brings dogwoods and redbuds, autumn brings the famous colour, and summer is warm and green but humid. Winter ice and fallen trees can close roads for days, and deer are a real hazard at dusk and dawn, so keep your speed sensible after the light fades.
t.boxley valley@36.0,-93.4:
A wide, quiet valley opens along Arkansas Highway 21 where the Buffalo National River comes down out of the Ozarks, and for a few miles the road runs through farmland that feels almost European in its calm. Boxley Valley is a historic district, with old farmsteads, a mill, a church, and fields bordered by split-rail fences, all protected as part of the national river. The mountains stand back on either side, and the light in the early morning can be remarkable.

The valley is also the best place in Arkansas to see elk. The animals were reintroduced here in the early 1980s, after having been wiped out in the state in the nineteenth century, and the herd has grown to a few hundred. In autumn, during the rut, bulls bugle across the fields and gather harems near the road. In the evening, you may find them grazing near the highway, and the sight of an animal that size close by is a thrill. Keep your distance, do not approach, and ride slowly, because they can step onto the road without warning.

The riding on Highway 21 is good rather than extreme, with pleasant curves, rolling hills, and views over the valley. It joins the steeper roads of the Ozark highlands, where the bends tighten and the forest closes in. Surface quality is generally fine, though shaded stretches can stay damp, and farm traffic and wandering wildlife call for attention. The best time is autumn for colour and elk, though spring has a freshness of its own, with wildflowers and bright new leaves.

Services here are sparse. Jasper, about twenty kilometres south, is a small town with a few shops and cafes, and Huntsville, farther east, is somewhat larger. Do not assume that fuel will be available at an hour of your choosing, and fill the tank before you commit to the valley. Water and snacks are easier to find than a full meal. The Buffalo River itself is clear, shallow, and good for a paddle or a paddle-free dip on a warm day, with limestone bluffs rising along its banks. Floods can rise quickly after storms, so heed the signs and keep clear of low crossings.
t.kronstadt@60.0,29.8:
Kronstadt sits on Kotlin Island, a long, narrow strip of land in the Gulf of Finland, about thirty kilometres west of Saint Petersburg, and for three centuries it has been the naval gatekeeper of the capital. Peter the Great founded the fortress in 1704, on a sandbank he had captured from the Swedes, and the harbour became the main base of the Russian Baltic Fleet. Forts rose on artificial islands across the shallow waters, stone batteries guarded the channel, and the town filled with sailors, officers and shipyards.

The history here is dramatic. In 1921, the sailors of Kronstadt, who had been among the most loyal supporters of the Bolsheviks in 1917, rose against the government, demanding free elections and an end to the monopoly of the Communist Party. The revolt was crushed after two weeks, by troops who crossed the ice, and it remains a bitter symbol of the early Soviet state. During the Second World War, the fleet defended Leningrad from this base, and the guns of the forts supported the besieged city. For decades, the island was a closed military zone, and it opened to visitors only in the 1990s.

The town today is a surprise. The streets are wide, with old naval buildings and warehouses, canals, and a great Naval Cathedral of Saint Nicholas, a domed building in neo-Byzantine style, completed in 1913 and recently restored, with a golden dome that is visible from the sea. The Italian Palace, built for Peter's friend Menshikov, and the old dry docks are worth a stop. Cobbled sections can be rough on a motorcycle, and the town has a slightly forgotten, faded feel.

The approach is by the flood barrier, a long causeway completed in the 2010s that protects Saint Petersburg from storm surges and carries a motorway across the gulf, with views of the sea on both sides. Wind can be fierce on the dam, so keep a firm grip. The weather is changeable, with fog, rain and sea mist. The best season is summer, with white nights, though the town can be busy at weekends.

Fuel is available in town, and there are cafés, shops and a few places to stay. Check the opening times for the cathedral and museums, and carry your passport, since ID is sometimes asked. Stand on the sea wall and look east. You can see the skyline of Saint Petersburg, shimmering in the haze.
t.central balkan peesh skali reserve@42.8,:
Peesh skali means singing rocks, after the way the wind howls and whistles through the cliffs and crags of this reserve on the slopes of the central Balkan range. It lies on the northern side of the main ridge, not far from Botev, at 2,376 metres the highest peak of the Balkan mountains, and it protects beech and spruce forests, alpine meadows and rocky slopes, part of Central Balkan National Park. Chamois live on the crags, and bears, wolves and golden eagles roam the area. Access to the reserve is restricted, but trails in the surrounding park offer spectacular walks.

On the southern side of the range, the town of Kalofer is the birthplace of Hristo Botev, the revolutionary poet who died fighting the Ottomans in 1876 and gave his name to the peak. Kalofer is also known for its lace and for the Epiphany tradition, when men dance in the icy river. To the north, the town of Apriltsi sits in a valley surrounded by forest, and Gabrovo, the main town of the region, is known for its humour and its House of Humour and Satire, a museum dedicated to jokes and cartoons.

The roads around here offer some of the best riding in Bulgaria. The Shipka pass, east of the reserve, crosses the Balkan range with hairpins, forests and views, and at the top stands a monument to the battles of the Russo-Turkish war of 1877. Nearby, the strange concrete saucer of the Buzludzha monument, built by the communist party, sits on a peak. The surfaces are variable, and fog and rain are common in the mountains. Summer is the best season for the high roads.

Gabrovo, about twenty-four kilometres away, is the main town for fuel, repairs and a hotel bed, and its House of Humour and Satire, a museum devoted to jokes and cartoons, is a cheerful antidote to monuments. Kalofer and Apriltsi cover the basics and have guesthouses that serve hearty home cooking. Kebapcheta, grilled minced-meat rolls, with a cold Bulgarian beer, are the classic end to a day in the mountains. The reserve itself is strictly protected; walk the park trails around it instead, and keep a close eye on the weather on the high ground.
t.the i repin estate the penates@60.2,29.9:
In 1903 the painter Ilya Repin, the most famous Russian artist of his day, moved to a wooden house in the village of Kuokkala on the Gulf of Finland, which he named the Penates, after the Roman household gods. He lived and worked there until his death in 1930, and after Finnish independence in 1917, he found himself living abroad, refusing invitations to return to the Soviet Union. The house, with its glass-roofed studio and eccentric architecture, was destroyed in the Second World War and rebuilt afterwards, and it is now a museum with many of his paintings and possessions.

Repin was famous for his hospitality, and his Wednesday gatherings attracted writers, artists and musicians, including Gorky, Mayakovsky and Chaliapin. He was also an advocate of vegetarianism and simple living, and his wife, Natalia Nordman, served guests meals of hay soup and vegetables, much to their amusement. The grounds, with paths, ponds and pavilions, are a pleasant place to walk, and Repin is buried in the park.

The coast of the Karelian Isthmus, along the Gulf of Finland, is a popular summer resort for the people of St Petersburg, with sandy beaches, pine forests and dachas. The road along the coast, from St Petersburg through Repino and Komarovo, where the poet Anna Akhmatova is buried, is pleasant, with views over the sea, but busy in summer.

Fuel and shops line the coast road through the resort district, and the city centre is roughly an hour back along the gulf. The museum is open to visitors, and the grounds, with their paths, ponds and pavilions, are a pleasant place to walk. The beaches along the coast are popular in summer, and the pine forests offer shade and quiet. Anyone considering a visit should check current government travel advice, which for many countries advises against all travel to Russia, and consider the legal and practical risks carefully.
t.central balkan dzhendema reserve@42.7,25:
Above the little town of Kalofer, the southern wall of the Balkan range rises almost vertically, cut by deep gorges with waterfalls and covered in old beech and fir forest, and up there lies the Dzhendema reserve, one of the strict nature reserves within Central Balkan National Park. The name is said to come from a Turkish word for hell, a fair description of its steep, wild terrain. Above the reserve, Botev Peak, the highest summit of the Balkan mountains at 2,376 metres, stands at the heart of the park. Bears, wolves, chamois and wild goats roam these slopes, and the old beech forests of the park are part of the transnational World Heritage site of the Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of Europe.

Kalofer has a special place in Bulgarian history as the birthplace of Hristo Botev, the revolutionary poet who died in 1876 fighting the Ottomans, and whose name was given to the highest peak. Karlovo, a few kilometres west, was the birthplace of Vasil Levski, the national hero of the liberation movement. Both towns lie in the Rose Valley, the broad valley south of the mountains, where fields of oil-bearing roses are harvested in late May and early June to produce rose oil, a precious ingredient for perfumes. In the early morning during the harvest, the scent hangs over the valley like a cloud.

The riding is excellent. The road through the Rose Valley, from Karlovo through Kalofer to Kazanlak, is a pleasant, gently winding route along the foot of the mountains, with views of the peaks rising above. From Karlovo, a road climbs north over the Troyan Pass, also called Beklemeto, through forest and open alpine meadows, with long sweeping descents and views on both sides of the range; to the east, the Shipka Pass, the scene of a famous battle in the Russo-Turkish War of 1877 to 1878, crosses the mountains to Gabrovo. Surfaces vary, and in winter the passes can be snowy, sometimes closed.

Karlovo, about fifteen kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Kalofer has a few shops and guesthouses. Try banitsa, a flaky pastry filled with cheese, and shopska salad with tomatoes, cucumbers and white cheese, and buy a small bottle of rose water or rose oil as a souvenir.
t.fort ino@60.2,29.5:
In pine woods on the northern shore of the Gulf of Finland, west of the resort strip of Zelenogorsk, lie the shattered concrete remains of Fort Ino. It was built from 1909 as part of the defences of Saint Petersburg, a key battery of Peter the Great's Naval Fortress, designed to close the gulf to enemy fleets with heavy guns. When Finland became independent, the fort ended up on Finnish territory, and under the Treaty of Tartu in 1920 its fortifications were to be dismantled, which is why what remains today is mostly blasted concrete, scattered among the trees and dunes.

The Karelian Isthmus here is a land of sand, pine and granite boulders left by the ice age glaciers, with long beaches on the gulf and lakes inland. It was Finnish territory until the Winter War and Second World War, and traces of Finnish farms, cemeteries and fortifications remain in the forests. Komarovo, a few kilometres east, is a resort village where the poet Anna Akhmatova spent her last summers and is buried.

The roads here run along the coast and through pine forests, mostly flat with gentle bends, and in summer they are busy with holidaymakers heading to the beaches and dachas. The coastal road is pleasant, with occasional views of the gulf, and smaller roads lead inland to lakes and villages. Surfaces vary, and sand can drift onto the road near the beaches.

The light on this coast is the thing people remember. On summer evenings the sun sinks slowly into the gulf toward Finland, the sand turns pink, and the pines throw long shadows across the ruins. Locals come out to swim in shallow, cool water that barely gets salty this far east in the Baltic. In winter the gulf freezes, and ice fishermen walk far out onto it.

Fuel and services are available in Zelenogorsk and Roshchino, ten kilometres away inland, while Molodyozhnoye, the nearest village, is small. The fort ruins are reached by forest paths and can be dangerous, with broken concrete, holes and rusted metal, so take care. Visitors from abroad face a changed political and practical situation in Russia, so official advice comes before any plan here.
t.central balkan sokolna reserve@42.7,25.1:
The Central Balkan National Park covers the high spine of the Stara Planina, the Balkan Mountains, which divide northern Bulgaria from the Thracian plain. Sokolna is one of the strict reserves within the park, on the steep southern slopes above Kalofer and Pavel Banya, where beech forests climb towards bare ridges and peaks. Its old beech woods are part of the World Heritage site of ancient beech forests, and the area is rich in wildlife, from bears and wolves to chamois and birds of prey.

The reserve itself is closed to vehicles, but the riding nearby is among the best in Bulgaria. The Shipka Pass road climbs from Kazanlak through tight hairpins and forested slopes to the monument at the top, then descends to Gabrovo on the north side. It is a steep, twisting road with good views, but the surface can be uneven and traffic heavy in summer. The road along the southern foot of the mountains, through the Rose Valley from Karlovo to Kazanlak, is flatter and faster, with stunning views of the mountains rising above. Spring and early summer are ideal, especially during the rose harvest, while winter can bring snow and closures on higher roads.

This area is steeped in history. Kalofer is the birthplace of Hristo Botev, the revolutionary poet who died fighting the Ottomans in 1876, and the town has a museum dedicated to him. Shipka Pass was the site of fierce battles during the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–78, which led to Bulgarian independence. The Rose Valley is famous for its rose oil, used in perfumes worldwide, and the Thracian tombs near Kazanlak, including one with remarkable frescoes on the World Heritage list, testify to an ancient civilisation.

The landscape changes dramatically with altitude, from orchards and fields in the valley to beech forests and alpine meadows on the slopes. The highest peak, Botev, rises to 2,376 metres and is often shrouded in cloud. In late May and June the valley is filled with the scent of roses, and the harvest is celebrated with festivals.

Kazanlak, about twenty-three kilometres away, is the main town with fuel, food and accommodation. Kalofer and Pavel Banya are smaller but have basic services. Try local specialities like banitsa and shopska salad, and do not leave without a bottle of rose liqueur or a pot of rose jam.
t.madara rider@43.3,27.1:
Above the village of Madara, on a vertical cliff about a hundred metres up, a horseman is carved into the rock, thrusting a spear at a lion that lies under his horse, while a dog runs behind. The Madara Rider is the only relief of its kind in Europe, made in the early eighth century by the first Bulgarian state, probably to celebrate a victory by Khan Tervel, and it is a rare relic of the pre-Christian era of the country. UNESCO listed it in 1979. Beside it are Greek inscriptions recording the deeds of Bulgarian khans, among the oldest written documents in the country.

The figure is not easy to see, because it has weathered badly, and the best way to appreciate it is to climb the wooden staircase that rises up the cliff, with a couple of hundred steps through beech and oak, until you stand opposite the relief. From the plateau above, the views over the Shumen plateau and the plains toward the Black Sea are wide. Caves in the cliff held a shrine in earlier times, and the plateau was once the site of a Thracian sanctuary and a Roman and medieval fortress.

For the ride, this is the heart of north-eastern Bulgaria, with a gentle countryside of fields, sunflowers and low hills, and the roads are straightforward. The main highway, the A2, runs to Varna on the coast, while the older roads through Shumen and Novi Pazar offer more interest, with shady villages, orchards and small climbs. Surfaces are sometimes rough, with patches and potholes, and lorries can be slow, so it pays to ride with care. Summers are hot and dry, spring and early autumn are best, and in winter the plains can be icy.

Kaspichan, a short distance away, has fuel and shops, and the larger town of Novi Pazar, ten kilometres off, has more choice. Shumen, a bit farther, is home to a well-known brewery, and also to the huge monument to the founding of the Bulgarian state. Try a shopska salad, with tomato, cucumber and white cheese, and a meal of grilled meat in a village restaurant, and carry water for the climb to the rock.
t.fort seraya loshad@60.0,29.2:
Along the southern shore of the Gulf of Finland, west of Saint Petersburg, a low strip of pine forest and sand runs for kilometres between the road and the sea. Fort Seraya Loshad, the Grey Horse, stands in this coastal country, eleven kilometres from the village of Lebyazhye, among a group of forts built for the defence of the capital and the naval base at Kronstadt.

The forts date from the early twentieth century, when Russia built a ring of concrete and steel batteries to protect the sea approaches to Saint Petersburg after the war with Japan. Seraya Loshad and its neighbour Krasnaya Gorka were part of this system, with heavy guns in turrets behind thick concrete. In June 1919, during the Civil War, the garrisons of both forts rose against the Bolsheviks, and the revolt was put down with the help of British naval action in the gulf and fighting by land. In the Second World War the area was the western end of the Oranienbaum pocket, a small coastal bridgehead around Oranienbaum that Soviet troops held throughout the siege of Leningrad, with the sea at their backs. Ruins of that history lie in the woods, and I cannot say what exactly remains accessible at the fort today, since parts of the coast are closed to the public.

On a motorcycle, the roads are mostly flat and straight, with a few bends where the road bends around villages and old estates. The coast road carries a steady flow of traffic, and in summer there are crowds of beach-goers heading for the sea. The Gulf is shallow and the water is cold, and in the early morning the light over the sea is flat and silvery. Winter is cold and grey, with snow and strong winds off the water, and the white nights of June give very long evenings.

Lebyazhye, a village of about five and a half thousand people, is the closest place for fuel and food, while Sosnovy Bor, a town of nearly seventy thousand, lies twelve kilometres away and has the nuclear power station that supplies much of the region. Bring mosquito repellent in summer, because the woods are damp and the insects are active. Regulations for travelling in the area, including border zones, can change, so check before you go.
t.petajavesi old church@62.3,25.2:
The lakeland of Central Finland is a place of low wooded ridges, narrow lakes and small farms, and Petäjävesi, a village of three and a half thousand people, lies on the shore of Lake Päijänne's northern arm, about twenty-five kilometres from Keuruu. Its old church, built entirely of pine logs, is one of the best-known wooden buildings in Europe and was inscribed by UNESCO in 1994.

The church was built between 1763 and 1765 by a local master carpenter, Jaakko Klemetinpoika Leppänen, to a design that mixes the traditions of Finnish log building with the shapes of the Baroque and Gothic styles known from stone churches elsewhere. Leppänen's son Erkki added the tower in 1821. The walls are hewn logs joined at the corners, the roof is covered in wooden shingles blackened with tar, and the whole building has a sturdy, handsome look, a little like a ship on dry land. Inside, the plain pews and the vaulted ceiling are simple and graceful, and in summer the church is open to visitors, with a small exhibition and guides. The smell of tar and old timber is part of the experience.

Riding in Finland is relaxed and orderly. The roads are well kept, speed limits are strict and speed cameras are common, and headlights must be on at all times. The scenery around Petäjävesi is a quiet repeat of lakes, spruce and birch, with long straights and gentle bends. Elk are a serious danger, especially at dusk and dawn from late summer onward, so slow down in forest sections and watch the verges. Mosquitoes and horseflies are active in midsummer, and in winter the roads can be icy and the days are very short.

The best time is June to August, when the light is long and the lakes are warm, with midsummer, the weekend closest to the 24th of June, a famous holiday when the whole country goes to its summer cottages. September brings the colours of autumn. Petäjävesi has shops, a petrol station and a cafe, and Keuruu, twenty-five kilometres away, is larger, with eleven thousand people, more fuel and a lakeside promenade. Try a fresh muikku, a small lake fish that is fried and served with potatoes, or a slice of rye bread with cheese, and drink coffee, which Finns take in vast quantities.
t.zelenogorsky@60.1,29.8:
The northern shore of the Gulf of Finland, west of Saint Petersburg, was for centuries the summer playground of the capital, and Zelenogorsk, which the Finns called Terijoki, was the best known of its resort towns. The coordinates put you in the pine woods just inland from the shore, and the towns of Kronstadt and Sestroretsk are each about nine or ten kilometres away.

Terijoki belonged to Finland between 1917 and 1940, when the border lay only a little further east, and the Finnish years left a mark in the wooden villas, the tidy gardens and the sandy beaches. Many of the houses that survive date from the early twentieth century, when Petersburg's artists and writers rented dachas here, and the resort had a casino and a train line. At the start of the Winter War, in late 1939, the Soviet Union announced a puppet government in Terijoki, and the town was ceded after the war. Sestroretsk, a little way east, has its own story. The town was founded by Peter the Great as an arms factory, and nearby, at Razliv, Lenin hid in a hut and a haystack in the summer of 1917 to escape arrest.

The Maritime Channel, mentioned on your ride, is the long dredged waterway that carries ships from the open gulf to the port of Saint Petersburg, and Kronstadt, on its island, was the main base of the Russian Baltic Fleet. The fort-island has a grim and fascinating history, with a naval cathedral, rows of old forts and the memory of the mutiny of 1921.

As a ride, the coast road is flat and mostly straight, passing through pines and over sand, and it is best on a weekday when the traffic is light. Weekend traffic to the beaches is heavy in July. Mosquitoes and ticks are a nuisance, the water is shallow and the sea cold, and in winter the gulf freezes, sometimes far out. The lovely season is late spring and early summer, when the lilac and bird-cherry blossom and the evenings stay light, and September is good for the colour.

Zelenogorsk has services, and the nearest bigger settlements, Sestroretsk and Kronstadt, have fuel stations and cafes, though access to Kronstadt has been restricted at times, so check. The area is a pleasant place for a swim in warm weather, a plate of smoked fish at a stall, and a walk along the dunes. Conditions for foreign visitors in Russia change, so look into the latest rules before you plan a ride here.
t.northern battery no 4@60.0,29.8:
Kotlin Island lies in the Gulf of Finland, at the entrance to the Neva, and its job for three centuries has been to guard St Petersburg from the sea. Peter the Great founded the naval base of Kronstadt here in 1704, and the island, long and narrow, was ringed with forts, batteries and artificial islands. The northern batteries, of which No. 4 is one, belong to that long chain, built in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries as the guns grew bigger and the ships more dangerous. They are low, grass-covered earthworks and brick casemates facing the water, and on grey days the place has a lonely, military feel. The sea is shallow here and often frozen in winter.

Kronstadt has a bigger place in history than its size would suggest. In 1921 its sailors, once the heroes of the revolution, rebelled against the Bolshevik government, and the uprising was crushed in a few days. The town's naval cathedral, a big domed building with a restored interior, stands in the centre, and a harbour of old dry docks and brick warehouses has been made into a quiet, interesting walk. For decades the island was closed to outsiders, and travel there was only opened in the 1990s.

A flood-protection barrier, completed in 2011, carries a road across the water from the mainland to Kotlin, and this is how most people arrive. The road is flat and fast, with the grey water on both sides and the horizon a thin line, and the wind is the main thing a rider will notice. On the island, the roads are straight and the surface is mixed. Summer evenings are very long this far north, and the white nights give a soft pearl light until after midnight. Winters are bitterly cold.

Access to some military areas can be restricted, and entry rules for visitors can change, so check what is allowed before you go. Kronstadt, a few kilometres away, has fuel and shops, and Gorskaya and Aleksandrovskaya are smaller. Midsummer is the best time for the light, and a day trip from Saint Petersburg is easy.
t.ancient city of nessebar@42.7,27.7:
Nessebar sits on a small rocky peninsula that sticks out into the Black Sea, joined to the mainland by a narrow causeway, and the whole of the old town is an open-air museum. Greek colonists from Megara founded it in the sixth century BC, calling it Mesembria, and it passed through Thracian, Roman, Byzantine, Bulgarian and Ottoman hands. Its position, with a good harbour and a defensible rock, made it a valued port for two and a half thousand years. UNESCO listed the old town in 1983.

The most striking monuments are the churches. At one time there were dozens on this tiny peninsula, and several survive in ruins or in good condition. The Church of Christ Pantocrator, from the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, has decorative bands of brick and stone and ceramic discs, the New Metropolis of Saint Stephen has beautiful frescoes, and the broken arches of the Old Metropolis, known as Saint Sophia, stand near the harbour. The houses on the cobbled lanes are in a style of the Bulgarian Revival, with a stone ground floor and an overhanging wooden upper storey, and the old wooden windmill on the seafront is a favourite photograph.

Be prepared for crowds. Sunny Beach, a huge resort with hotels and nightclubs, begins just up the coast, and in July and August the narrow lanes of the old town are packed with visitors and souvenir stalls. The best times are early spring, May and September, when the sea is warm and the town is calmer. Early mornings and evenings are lovely, with the light turning the stone gold and the water silver.

The causeway entrance is a bottleneck, and parking close to the old town is limited, so park on the new town side and walk across. Fuel is available in the new part of Nesebar and in the surrounding towns of Ravda and Sveti Vlas, and Burgas, the main city of the coast, is about half an hour south. The coast road is flat and busy in summer, with plenty of traffic, so those who want a good ride should head inland toward the hills of the Balkan range.

Fish is the obvious meal here, grilled or fried, with a shopska salad of tomato, cucumber and white cheese, and a glass of local wine or rakia. The ride heads inland to Sveshtari, in the north-east, where a Thracian tomb of the third century BC has remarkable carved figures and paintings.
t.the cemetery of the village of komarovo@:
Anna Akhmatova is buried here. The cemetery of Komarovo is a small, quiet graveyard among pines on the Karelian Isthmus, on the shore of the Gulf of Finland about forty kilometres north-west of Saint Petersburg, and her grave, a simple stone with a cross, is the one that people come to find. She died in 1966, and loved the little cottage she was given in the village, which she called her Booth. The cemetery also holds the grave of the scholar Dmitry Likhachev, and a scattering of writers, artists and scientists who spent their summers in this dacha colony, once reserved for the Soviet cultural elite.

The village used to be called Kellomäki and belonged to Finland until the Winter War of 1939 and 1940, when the isthmus passed to the Soviet Union. You can still feel the Finnish origins in the layout of the roads and the old wooden villas hidden among the trees. Riding here is a pleasure of pine-scented air and quiet lanes. The main road along the coast, the Primorskoe highway, is busy and fast, but the side roads through Komarovo are narrow, tree-lined and slow, with sand and pine needles on the surface, so go gently. Summer evenings in the white-night season are magical, and autumn colours of birch and aspen are rich.

Zelenogorsk, about five kilometres away, has nearly fifteen thousand people and is the sensible place for fuel and food. It was also Finnish once, as Terijoki, and has a seaside promenade. Komarovo itself has a few cafes and shops, but the options are limited. The nearby Road of Life, a memorial route, recalls the winter of 1941 to 1942, when supplies reached besieged Leningrad across the ice of Lake Ladoga, a story told here with solemnity.

Visit with respect. This is a place of mourning and remembrance rather than a tourist stop, and people walk through it quietly. Take off your helmet, walk among the pines, and let the stillness settle. The sea is just beyond the trees, and on a calm day you can hear it.
t.puolakka oravivuori@61.9,25.5:
Finland's lakeland is a country of water more than of land, and Päijänne, the second largest lake in the country, runs south from here for over a hundred kilometres in long, island-dotted fingers. Oravivuori, Squirrel Hill, is a forested rise near Puolakka in the Korpilahti district, now part of Jyväskylä, and the lookout on the hill gives a wide view over spruce, pine and the shining lake beyond. The label points to a hill rather than a monument, so think of it as a place to climb, look and breathe.

The riding is calm and rhythmic. Finnish country roads are well surfaced, with gentle rises and falls through birch and pine, and the lake appears and disappears between the trees. Speed limits are strictly enforced and fines are scaled to income, so keep to the signs. Elk are the real hazard, especially at dawn and dusk, when they step out of the forest without warning, and the warning signs are not decoration. Summer days are very long, with light until late, and September brings crisp air and colour, but frost can arrive early, so a warm layer is sensible.

Korpilahti has just over five thousand people and is the practical place for fuel and food, about ten kilometres away. Luhanka, farther off, is much smaller. Fuel stations in rural Finland are often automated and card-only, so carry a card that works, and do not let the tank run low. Petäjävesi, a short ride to the west, has a remarkable old wooden church, built in the 1760s by a local farmer-builder in a mixture of log construction and Lutheran form, and now on the UNESCO list. It is a small, plain building of dark timber, and it rewards a visit.

Do as the Finns do and finish the day with a sauna and a swim, if you can find a lakeside cabin. Failing that, a coffee and a cinnamon bun at a village cafe makes a respectable second best. The silence at dusk, with the lake turning pewter and a loon calling somewhere in the reeds, is one of the great pleasures of the north.
t.fort totleben@60.1,29.8:
Eduard Totleben was the engineer who held Sevastopol in the Crimean War, and the Russian navy named a fort after him in the ring of defences that guards Saint Petersburg from the sea. Fort Totleben, along with its neighbour Fort Peter I, belongs to the northern line of fortifications built on shoals in the Gulf of Finland, in the nineteenth century, to protect the approaches to Kronstadt and the capital. The coordinates fall on the shore near Sestroretsk, from where the forts can be glimpsed on a clear day as dark shapes on the horizon, but most of them are not open to casual visitors.

The ride along this stretch of coast is calm and easy. The Primorskoe highway runs along the north shore of the gulf, through pine woods and past dachas, with a decent surface, moderate bends and occasional speed cameras. Traffic builds on summer weekends, when the city flees to the beach, and the best time to ride is early on a weekday morning. The water is shallow here and freezes in winter, and when the ice is thick people walk out onto it, though I would not recommend riding there.

Sestroretsk, with over thirty-seven thousand people, is a short ride away and is where you buy fuel and food. Peter the Great founded it in 1714 as an arms factory town, and a lake created for the works, Razliv, is also known for a small hut where Lenin hid in the summer of 1917 before the October Revolution, now a museum. Razliv itself is a little place of about twelve hundred people.

If you want an image to carry away, stand on the shore near sunset and look out at the long horizon of the gulf, where the forts sit like low ships at anchor. They were built for a war that never came in the form their designers feared, and the gulf is left to the gulls. The sand is pale, the pine trees tall and the light, in summer, almost endless.
t.the park dubki@60.1,29.9:
Peter the Great loved oak, because oak meant ships, and the little park of Dubki, whose name means little oaks, is said to date back to the trees he ordered planted near his arms-making settlement at Sestroretsk. Whatever the truth of the exact planting, the park is a pleasant tract of old trees on sandy soil, with paths, ponds and the slow rhythm of a town that has long been a seaside resort. Sestroretsk, on the Gulf of Finland, became a fashionable spa at the end of the nineteenth century, and its shore of shallow water and fine sand still draws crowds in summer.

The riding is unhurried. The Ropshinskoe highway of the label belongs to a different part of the region, but the roads around Sestroretsk are flat, straight and shaded by pines and oaks. The surface is mostly good, with some frost-damaged patches after winter, and traffic can be heavy in July and August. You are better off in May or September, when the beach is quiet and the light is clear. Look out for cyclists and walkers on the lanes by the park, as the whole community seems to use them.

Sestroretsk is a town of over thirty-seven thousand, so fuel, food and groceries are within easy reach, only about two kilometres from the park. The old factory buildings, the lake called Razliv, and the sand dunes by the shore make for an interesting afternoon, and a seafront promenade offers cafes for a coffee stop. The town was also one of the places where the Karelian Isthmus front stabilised in the Second World War, and traces of defence lines are still visible in the woods if you know where to look.

A good way to enjoy Dubki is to leave the bike, walk under the oaks and listen to the wind in the leaves. In autumn the leaves turn bronze, and the ground is covered with acorns that crunch underfoot. It is an ordinary park by Saint Petersburg's standards, but its oaks carry a link to a man who wanted a navy and began by planting trees.
t.northern battery no 1@60.0,29.8:
Kotlin Island is a long, thin sliver of land in the Gulf of Finland, and Kronstadt, its fortress-town, was founded by Peter the Great in 1704 to guard the sea approaches to his new capital. It became the base of the Russian Baltic Fleet, and ring after ring of forts, batteries and ramparts was built on the island and on artificial islands around it. The Northern Battery No. 1 is one of those fortifications, a low military work on the north shore of Kotlin, part of a defensive system that went on being added to for more than two centuries.

Today the island is linked to the mainland by a long flood barrier, a vast engineering project completed around 2011 to protect Saint Petersburg from storm surges. A road runs along the barrier, and the crossing is one of the strangest rides in the region, with the gulf stretching out on one side and the open sea on the other. Weather can change quickly on the dam, with strong winds and sudden rain, so check conditions and be prepared for gusts that push a bike sideways. Within Kronstadt the streets are straight and wide, and traffic is light.

Kronstadt itself has about forty-three thousand people and is a place with services, shops and cafes, about four kilometres from the battery. For fuel, use stations on the mainland side before crossing, or in Kronstadt town. Gorskaya, farther along the coast, is smaller. The town's great naval cathedral, with its huge gilded dome, was restored in the 2010s and stands as one of the city's most visible landmarks. In 1921, the sailors of Kronstadt rose against the Bolshevik government in a rebellion that was crushed within days, a bloody episode that still shapes the town's memory.

If you visit the battery, be aware that access to military zones in Russia can be restricted, so check what is open before you go. The shore here is windy and bleak, with rusted iron, granite blocks and shallow grey water. It is a stark, impressive place, and a reminder of how much effort was spent defending a city that sits so exposed on the sea.
t.tolbukhin lighthouse on tolbukhin island:
Ships have been guided by a light on Tolbukhin island for about three centuries, and it is one of those places that makes more sense on a chart than on a road. The island lies in the Gulf of Finland, south-west of Kronstadt and out in the shallow channel that leads to Saint Petersburg, and the lighthouse on it marks the southern passage into the Neva Bay. The surrounding waters are shallow, and in the grey light of autumn the sea and the sky merge into a single pale band.

You will not ride to the lighthouse. It stands on an island that is part of the fortified system of Kotlin and Kronstadt, and the nearest point you can reach by road lies on the coast or the island's shore, looking out across the water. Even so, the label is a reminder of how this whole landscape was shaped by the sea and by defence. Peter the Great founded Saint Petersburg in 1703 and the fortress island of Kotlin, with its forts and batteries, was built to guard the approach from Sweden.

The coast around here is flat and green, with pine, birch and reed beds meeting a shallow sea that freezes in winter. In summer the light stays soft until very late, the famous white nights, and in autumn the gulls and ducks move through in great numbers. The air smells of salt, wet wood and diesel from the harbour. It is not dramatic scenery, but it has a quiet northern beauty.

Riding in this area means long, straight roads with modest traffic and occasional rough patches. The Dam, the huge flood barrier that stretches across the gulf and carries a motorway, is the only land link between Kotlin and the mainland. Wind off the water can be strong, and fog sometimes rolls in without warning. Check the weather before you set off and keep your speed measured.

Kronstadt, eight kilometres away, is the town for fuel and food, with forty thousand people and a long naval tradition. Bring warm layers even in summer, because the wind off the gulf is cool.
A mill in the middle of a forest is a strange thing to find in Finland, until you remember that the forest was the point. The Verla Groundwood and Board Mill, in Kymenlaakso in south-eastern Finland, was built in the 1870s beside a waterfall, where the river provided power and the surrounding woods provided the raw material. It made groundwood pulp and cardboard until it closed in 1964, and what remains is one of the best-preserved examples of a small wood-processing village in the world, which is why UNESCO listed it in 1996.

The buildings are mostly wooden, painted in dark red or ochre, with tall brick chimneys and a pair of steep-roofed mill halls that stand beside the rapids. The workers lived in the village, which had its own school, shops and a sauna, and the company's owners lived in a grander house nearby. It has the compact, carefully organised feel of a place built for a purpose, and it is easy to imagine the noise of the machinery and the smell of wet wood.

The landscape around is gentle and green. Forests of spruce, pine and birch roll away on every side, broken by small lakes and farmland, and the light on a summer evening seems to last for ever. Moose, which Finns call hirvi, live in these woods, and so do deer and wolves, though you are far more likely to meet a moose than anything else on the road, especially at dusk.

For a rider the roads here are smooth, quiet and well signed. They run in long, wooded curves with plenty of visibility, and the speed limits, usually eighty on country roads, are enforced by cameras and police. Keep an eye out for wildlife, particularly at dawn and dusk, and for cyclists. Summer is the season, with long days and warm weather, and September can be golden, though mornings turn cold quickly.

Jaala is a small village, and Kouvola, twenty-two kilometres away, is the nearest sizeable town, with fuel, shops and restaurants. Fill up there. The mill has a museum and a café in season, so check opening times before arriving.
t.northern battery no 2@60.0,29.8:
Forts are places for people who like their history with a view of the sea, and Kotlin island has more of them than most. Northern Battery No. 2 is part of the chain of defences that guarded the northern channel into the Gulf of Finland, and it dates from the great programme of fortification that Russia undertook in the nineteenth century to protect Kronstadt and, behind it, the capital. The batteries line the island's northern shore, low, squat and half buried in the pines.

Kotlin is a long, thin island, about twelve kilometres from end to end, and it was strategic from the moment Peter the Great took it from Sweden. He built the first fort in 1704, and over the next two centuries the island was ringed with forts, some on artificial islets in the water and others along the shoreline. By the late nineteenth century it was one of the most heavily fortified places in Europe. The ruins and surviving works have a stark, overgrown beauty, with concrete and brick softened by moss and birch scrub.

The island is reached by the road across the Dam, which crosses the gulf in a series of embankments and bridges, with a tunnel under the main shipping channel, and carries the ring road around Saint Petersburg. On the island itself the roads are flat, straight and generally quiet, with views of the water through the trees. Surfaces vary, and winter frost leaves ruts and potholes by spring. Wind can be strong, and in summer the evenings are very long.

Access to some of the forts is limited, and others are in ruinous condition, so look carefully at local information before venturing off the road. Some parts of the island are military zones, and signs should be taken seriously. Use caution around crumbling masonry and never enter unstable structures.

Kronstadt, four kilometres away, is a town of forty-three thousand people, with fuel, shops and cafés. A walk along the harbour at sunset, with ships heading out to the gulf, is the best way to end a day here. Pack a windproof jacket, because the gulf breeze can chill even in July.
t.fort kronshlot@60.0,29.7:
Fort Kronshlot is a stone fortress sitting on an artificial island in the middle of the water, and it has been there, in one form or another, since 1704. Peter the Great ordered it built to guard the shallow channel to the new city of Saint Petersburg, and the first version was a wooden tower on piles driven into the seabed and filled with stone. The name comes from the German for crown castle. The current structure is mostly of the nineteenth century, a long oval of brick and granite with gun casemates facing the water.

Kronshlot sits two kilometres from the town of Kronstadt, which is just far enough to feel remote and just close enough to see. Together with the other forts of Kotlin, it was part of a system that made the capital almost impregnable from the sea. The system was tested during the Crimean War, when British and French ships approached and prudently turned away, and again during the world wars. Today the fort is mostly empty, and the waters around it are favoured by fishermen and the occasional rowing club.

The ride to Kronstadt along the Dam is an experience of its own. For about twenty kilometres you cross the gulf on a causeway with water on both sides, passing the sluice gates and the great ship passages that keep the city safe from storm surges. The road is straight and smooth, the wind can be fierce, and the horizon is huge. In clear weather you can see Kronstadt's gold dome from far away, and when mist rolls in the whole scene turns to pearl.

Autumn storms can push the sea high against the embankments, and in winter the ice can stretch to the horizon. Spring and summer are easiest, with warm sun, long evenings and light traffic outside rush hours. Observe the speed limits and look out for cameras.

Kronstadt itself has fuel, food and shops, and the harbour area has cafés where you can sit with a view of the water and the forts. A bag with a warm layer is a good idea even in summer, since the gulf breeze can be chilly.
t.forts of the island kotlin@60.0,29.7:
Kotlin island carries so many forts that the usual way to describe it is as a single stone ship moored in the middle of the gulf. The whole island is fortified, and you can see the evidence from the water, from the road and from the air: low batteries, round towers, harbour walls and the great forts built on artificial islands in the shallows. Many carry the names of tsars and grand dukes, and some, like the fort known as Alexander I, have a more sinister reputation, since it was used as a research station for plague bacteria in the early twentieth century and is still called the Plague Fort.

The stretch labelled here lies a couple of kilometres from the centre of Kronstadt, and the name refers to a dacha, a country house, that once belonged to a member of the nobility. These dachas appeared along the island's edge in the nineteenth century, when the defences were already old and Kronstadt had become a place for naval officers to live with their families. Some of the old wooden houses survive, with carved window frames and steep roofs, and they give the area a different mood from the grim, grey forts.

The defences were built for a reason: Russia's capital was only a day's sail from the open sea, and the shallow gulf made the channel past Kotlin the only deep route. A fleet that wanted to attack Saint Petersburg had to pass under these guns. The forts worked, and no enemy fleet ever got through.

The roads on Kotlin are flat, mostly straight, and quiet outside the town. Surfaces are patchy, wind off the water can be strong, and in winter the ice and snow make riding impractical. Between May and September the long evenings give a lot of time for exploring, and sunsets over the gulf are spectacular.

Kronstadt, two and a half kilometres away, has fuel, cafés and shops. Take warm clothing, as the wind from the water is cool even in summer. Some forts are accessible by boat tours in the warmer months, while others are closed or hazardous, so check what is possible before setting out.
t.the historical part of the town of krons:
Kronstadt's gold dome is visible from a long way off, and it belongs to the Naval Cathedral of Saint Nicholas, a great Byzantine-style church that was finished in 1913 for the sailors of the Baltic Fleet. The Soviets turned it into a cinema and then a sports hall, and a long restoration returned it to its original purpose in 2013. It now stands in the centre of a town that looks like an eighteenth-century naval base surrounded by sea.

The town was founded in 1704, as the fortress of Kronshlot's partner on the island of Kotlin, and its name means Crown Town.
