For most of the following three centuries it was the home of the Russian Baltic Fleet, and its harbours, canals and parade grounds still bear the marks of that history. Peter the Great's dry dock, an enormous stone basin dug in the early eighteenth century, is among the oldest in the world, and the Italian Palace, built for Prince Menshikov, is among the first buildings erected on the island. The historic centre was included in the UNESCO listing of Saint Petersburg in 1990.

In March 1921, Kronstadt's sailors rose against the Bolshevik government, demanding free elections and an end to grain requisitions. They were crushed after a brutal assault across the ice, and the episode marked a turning point in the revolution. During the Soviet era the town was closed to outsiders, and it is only in recent decades that it has been open to visitors again.

Today Kronstadt is a quiet, rather melancholy place, with wide streets, peeling plaster and the sound of gulls. The ride from the mainland, across the Dam, takes you into a flat, windy landscape with the sea always in view, and the town itself is small enough to explore on foot after parking the bike. The best time to come is on a clear day in summer, when the dome shines.

With forty-three thousand people, Kronstadt has fuel, supermarkets, cafés and basic accommodation. Wear a windproof layer, as the breeze from the gulf is often cold, and carry a photo ID, since some parts of the island remain military.
t.northern battery no 7@60.0,29.9:
Not every stop on a route has a story that belongs to one fort, and this one belongs to a coastline. The north shore of the Gulf of Finland, between Sestroretsk and Lisy Nos, is a flat, sandy and pine-covered strip of land that was once Finnish territory, and the batteries and forts built on it, including the one the label calls Fort Constantin, were part of the same defensive system that guarded Kronstadt from the other side. The names Gorskaya and Tarkhovka belong to the settlements around, and the Dam, the huge flood barrier that links the island with the mainland, lands at this shore.

The country here is typical of the Karelian Isthmus: sandy soil, pine woods, birch groves, heather and low dunes beside the sea. In summer the shallow water warms quickly and the beaches fill up at weekends, while in winter the sea freezes and people walk or ski across the ice. Berries and mushrooms grow in the forest, and in autumn locals can be seen carrying baskets along the roadsides.

Close by lies Razliv, a lake near Sestroretsk where Lenin hid in a hut in the summer of 1917, avoiding arrest. The hut and its sheltered haystack setting have been a museum since the Soviet era, and the place is still on the tourist trail. Sestroretsk itself has a Russian history of its own, beginning with an arms factory that Peter the Great founded in the early eighteenth century, and becoming a resort town in the nineteenth.

For the rider this is a flat and often busy region. Roads are generally in good condition, but traffic in summer can be thick, with holidaymakers heading for the beach. The best time is on a weekday morning, when the pine woods are fresh and the air smells of resin and sea. Winter riding is not a good idea, since ice and snow cover the roads.

Tarkhovka and Gorskaya are small settlements, while Sestroretsk and Zelenogorsk offer larger shops and fuel. Fill up before you go too far along the coast. Remember mosquito repellent in summer, since the damp woods breed clouds of them.
t.fortress of suomenlinna@60.1,25.0:
Suomenlinna is a fortress on a cluster of islands in front of Helsinki, reached in about fifteen minutes by public ferry from the Market Square. The Swedes began building it in 1748, when Finland was part of their kingdom and the Russian threat was growing, and they called it Sveaborg, the Fortress of the Swedes. The architect Augustin Ehrensvard designed the plan, and he is buried on the island. Granite ramparts, bastions, tunnels and storehouses are laid out among rocky islets, and a wide-angled view of the fortress from the sea is impressive.

The fortress was meant to be impregnable, but in 1808, during the war between Sweden and Russia, it surrendered after a short siege, and Finland passed to Russia. The Russians expanded the base, and it remained a garrison until Finland became independent in 1917, when it was renamed Suomenlinna, the Fortress of Finland. Later it was used as a military base, a prison and a training ground, and in 1991 it was inscribed by UNESCO. Today, about eight hundred people live on the islands, in old barracks and workers' houses, and there are museums, cafes, studios and a submarine, Vesikko, which you can climb into.

The atmosphere is relaxed. Paths run along the walls, with views over the Baltic, and families picnic on the grass slopes. In summer, the days are long, with light until near midnight, and in winter, the islands are quiet and frozen. Seagulls, wind and the smell of salt are constant.

For riders, the motorcycle stays on the mainland, since the ferry carries foot passengers and bicycles rather than motor vehicles. You can park near the Market Square and walk to the ferry pier. Helsinki has fuel at stations around the city, and the harbour area has cafes and restaurants. The route here connects to the ferries from Tallinn, so riders often arrive after crossing the Gulf of Finland. Weather is changeable, with wind off the sea, and a warm layer is useful even in summer. Allow at least half a day for the island, and take food if you want to picnic.
t.fort paul i@60.0,29.7:
To the Russian navy, Kronstadt is the fortress island of Kotlin in the eastern Gulf of Finland, and the forts scattered across the water around it were built to stop any enemy from approaching St Petersburg by sea. Fort Paul I, named after Peter the Great's great-grandson, is one of the numerous artificial islands and shore works in that defensive ring, and the pin lies about three and a half kilometres from Kronstadt and eight from Lomonosov on the mainland coast. I do not know exactly what you can see from this point, and access to many of the forts has been restricted or dangerous for years, so treat the stop as a view of the coast and the water rather than a visit.

Lomonosov, the town to the west, was once Oranienbaum, the estate of Prince Menshikov, Peter's favourite, and later of Peter III. During the siege of Leningrad in 1941 to 1944 a small stretch of this coast, known as the Oranienbaum Bridgehead, was held by Soviet troops against the German army, cut off from the city by the sea and supplied by ships across the gulf. The memory of that struggle is strong here, and monuments dot the roads. The route that mentions Oranienbaum Springboard refers to this episode.

The ride is flat and coastal. The road follows the shore through pine and birch woods, with glimpses of the water and the low outline of Kronstadt on the horizon, and the surface is mostly smooth. Traffic is heavy near the towns and light between them. In winter the Gulf freezes and the forts stand in a field of white, while in summer the white nights give a long, soft twilight. Wind off the water can be strong.

Fuel is easiest in Kronstadt or Lomonosov, both towns of more than forty thousand people, with garages and shops. In Lomonosov you can visit the palace-park ensemble of Oranienbaum, which includes the Chinese Palace, and a café or two serve simple meals. Check current access rules for any coastal area before you go, since parts of this coast are restricted, and carry your documents.
t.northern battery no 5@60.0,29.9:
On the northern shore of the Gulf of Finland, the Primorskoye Highway runs from St Petersburg through a string of resort villages, pine woods and sandy beaches toward Zelenogorsk and Vyborg. Northern Battery No. 5 belongs to the other side of the story, the chain of coastal defences that once guarded the sea approach to the city. The pin lies about six kilometres from Gorskaya and Aleksandrovskaya and just under seven from Kronstadt, which is visible across the water on a clear day. The exact condition of the battery, and whether it is open, I cannot say, and many such works are overgrown or fenced.

The route ties the battery to the Blockade Ring, the series of monuments around St Petersburg that mark the line where the Soviet army held the Germans during the siege of Leningrad, which lasted from September 1941 to January 1944. Nearly a million civilians died, mostly of hunger and cold, in one of the longest and deadliest sieges in history. The memorials are in the form of obelisks, tanks on plinths and plain stone markers, and they stand at crossroads and on hilltops around the city. They are sober places, and visitors are expected to behave quietly.

As a ride, the coastal road is fast and flat, with pine forest on one side and the sea on the other. The Primorskoye Highway is busy in summer, when city dwellers head for the beaches and dachas, but side roads through the woods are quieter. The sand is pale and the sky is wide, and the water is shallow and cold. In June and July the white nights keep the sky pale until midnight. In winter, ice and snow make riding impractical.

Fuel is available at garages along the highway and in Kronstadt, a town of forty-three thousand people. The villages along the coast have small shops and cafés that open in the summer season. Wear insect repellent in the woods in July, and carry water. If you plan to explore any military ruins, take care, since concrete and rusted metal can be hazardous.
t.fort alexander i@60.0,29.7:
Fort Alexander I stands in the water about three kilometres from Kronstadt, a low, oval stone fort built in the nineteenth century as part of the sea defences of St Petersburg. It is better known by another name, the Plague Fort, because at the end of the century the Russian authorities installed a laboratory here to study plague and develop vaccines, working in isolation on a site that could be reached only by boat. The island setting made sense, since a lab handling deadly bacteria needed to be separated from the mainland, and the work done here was part of the early history of research on infectious disease in Russia.

Today the fort is a ruin, and the pin marks a viewpoint on the shore from which you can see it and other forts of the Kronstadt system. Several of them stand along the line of the sea channel, and their dark outlines on the water at dusk give the Gulf of Finland a melancholy beauty. In winter, when the water freezes, the forts stand in a flat white plain. The route that links this stop to the Zinoviev datcha and the Steinbock-Fermor estate takes you through the wooded north coast, where aristocratic summer houses were built in the nineteenth century.

Riding here is a matter of flat, easy roads through the pine and birch forests of the coast. The surface is generally good, and traffic is moderate except on summer weekends. Since the opening of the flood barrier, the Dam, in the early 2010s, a road connects Kronstadt to the mainland, so that the island, long a closed naval town, is within reach of an ordinary road trip. Wind can be sharp, and the sea mist rolls in without warning.

Fuel is available in Kronstadt, only three kilometres away, and in Lomonosov, nearly ten. Both have cafés and shops. Access to the forts themselves is limited, and the sea is cold and treacherous even in summer, so do not attempt to reach them by boat without a licensed operator. Check local rules for the shore zone, and carry your passport and documents.
t.st louis@38.6,-90.2:
St. Louis is a river city with a very large arch in it. The Gateway Arch, designed by Eero Saarinen and finished in 1965, rises 630 feet on the west bank of the Mississippi, a catenary curve of stainless steel that is the tallest monument in the United States and one of the most recognisable. It marks the city's historic role as the gateway to the West, the starting point for settlers, trappers and explorers, including Lewis and Clark, who set out up the Missouri in 1804 from a camp not far north. At its feet, a museum tells the story of westward expansion, and a tram carries visitors to the top.

The city has a rich and sometimes difficult past. The courthouse downtown was the site of the Dred Scott trial, a milestone in the road to the Civil War. The 1904 World's Fair and the Olympic Games were held here, and left behind a legacy of grand parks and museums, including a free zoo. Beer is a local institution, with the great Anheuser-Busch brewery south of downtown, and the food has its own identity: toasted ravioli, gooey butter cake, and St. Louis-style pizza, which is thin and crisp and covered in a processed cheese called Provel that locals adore and visitors argue about.

For Route 66 riders, St. Louis is a major junction. The old road crossed the Mississippi on the Chain of Rocks Bridge, north of the city, a long steel span with a distinctive bend in the middle, now closed to cars but open to walkers and cyclists. The route then wound through city streets, past old diners, motels and neon signs, and out through the suburbs toward Missouri's Ozark hills. A famous frozen custard stand on Chippewa Street, a Route 66 landmark, draws crowds on summer evenings. It is a city for slow exploration of the old road, rather than speed, as traffic is heavy and the road passes through many stoplights.

With over three hundred thousand people in the city and many more in the metro area, fuel, parking and lodging are no problem. Downtown parking is metered, and the interstates are busy at rush hour. Summers are hot and humid, with thunderstorms, while spring and autumn are more pleasant. Take care on the surface streets near the old road, as potholes and railroad tracks are common, and some neighbourhoods are less welcoming than others, so keep an eye on the bike.
t.cuba missouri@38.1,-91.4:
Cuba, Missouri, is a small town of about three and a half thousand people in the Ozark foothills, and it has turned itself into the Mural City of Route 66. More than a dozen big paintings cover the walls of old buildings, showing the history of the town, the railroad, the highway and the people, and the effect is cheerful and slightly surreal, like a gallery laid out along a main street. The town is said to take its name from the island of Cuba.

The old road runs right through, and the best of the Route 66 relics are close by. The Wagon Wheel Motel, built in 1936 with its neon sign and stone cabins, claims to be the oldest operating motel on the road in Missouri, and it is a pleasure to see it still taking guests. A few miles east, at Fanning, a rocking chair more than forty feet high, the biggest in the world, stands outside an old gas station and souvenir stop, and it is almost impossible to resist stopping for a photograph. Nearby, the town of St. James produces wine in the Ozark vineyards.

For a rider, the old road here is a pleasure. It rolls through wooded hills and over small ridges, with gentle bends, fields of corn and hay, and small towns with old red-brick fronts. The surface varies from smooth modern tarmac to old concrete, and traffic is light on the stretches that run beside Interstate 44. Speed limits are low, and local police enforce them, so there is no need to hurry. The Meramec River, a few miles south near Steelville, is a popular place for float trips, and a swim on a hot day is a good break.

Fuel is available in Cuba itself, and there are cafes and diners serving fried chicken, biscuits and gravy, and slices of pie. Summer is hot and humid, with thunderstorms, so ride early, and autumn, when the oaks and hickories turn red and gold, is the best season. After a day on the road, a night in a vintage motel, with the neon buzzing outside and a cicada chorus in the trees, is the right way to finish.
t.russellville@35.3,-93.1:
Russellville sits in the Arkansas River Valley between two very different landscapes, the flat, farmed bottomland to the south and the rugged Boston Mountains to the north. It is a university and industrial town of about twenty-nine thousand people, home to Arkansas Tech University, with a downtown of old brick buildings, a nuclear power plant on the river and the broad water of Lake Dardanelle, created by a dam on the Arkansas River in the 1960s. It is the sort of place where a ride along Scenic Highway 7 makes its decision about direction.

The town marks the gateway to the Ozarks. North of here the land rises quickly, and the highway climbs through hardwood forests of oak and hickory, with sandstone bluffs, deep hollows and long ridgelines. Mount Nebo, a flat-topped mountain southeast of the town, has a state park with trails and views over the valley, and Petit Jean Mountain, further east, has a lodge and a waterfall that drops into a gorge. The Arkansas River is wide and slow here, and in autumn the whole valley glows with colour.

Highway 7 is widely praised as one of the most scenic roads in the United States, and the first miles heading north from town give you a taste of it. The road narrows, starts to curve and climbs into the hills, with a good surface and generous bends. Traffic can be heavy at weekends in autumn, when leaf-watchers are out, and logging trucks and cyclists share the road, so patience is useful. Summer is hot and humid, with thunderstorms, while spring brings dogwood and redbud, and winter can leave ice on the higher sections.

Fuel and food are easy in Russellville, with plenty of choice along Interstate 40 and Arkansas Avenue, including local barbecue and diner breakfasts. It is smart to fill the tank and eat here, because the road north has stretches with few services. Dover and Pottsville are small towns nearby, and the next big town is Harrison, much farther up. Take water, check the weather and enjoy the start of a good road.
t.jasper arkansas@36.0,-93.2:
Jasper is a courthouse square with a handful of shops and cafés in the middle of the Boston Mountains, and it is the finish line for a ride that has earned its sit-down. Newton County has fewer people than almost anywhere in Arkansas, and the village, a few hundred strong, is the county seat in the way small places often are, with a stone-fronted square, a pharmacy and a long front porch of a restaurant that has fed travellers since 1909. Harrison, twenty-six kilometres to the north, is the nearest town of any size.

The road that brings you here, Highway 7, comes down from the Arkansas River Valley over a series of ridges, through forests of oak and hickory, with sandstone bluffs along the shoulders and long views over hollows that go blue in the haze. The Boston Mountains are the highest part of the Ozarks, a deeply cut plateau rather than a true range, and the roads follow the ridgelines and drop into valleys in a way that gives the whole route its rhythm. Dogwoods flower in April, and in late October the hillsides turn a deep rust and gold.

Around Jasper lies the Buffalo National River, the first river in the United States to be protected under the national river designation, in 1972, and it runs clear and green between limestone bluffs. Canoes drift through in spring and early summer, when the water is high enough. A short drive away, Boxley Valley holds a herd of elk reintroduced in the 1980s, and in the cool of the morning or evening you may see them grazing beside the road, which is a good reason to ride with a little caution. The Little Buffalo, the Ponca bluffs and the old Boxley mill give the area a settled, quiet beauty.

Jasper has fuel, but check your tank earlier in the day because hours are short in the evening. Rain can come in fast, and the shaded bends are slippery with wet leaves in autumn. Order something fried and ask the person at the next table where they would ride tomorrow.
t.sile coast@41.2,29.6:
Şile is a small town on the Black Sea coast of Istanbul province, about seventy kilometres from the city centre, and for the city's riders it is the nearest place where you can smell the sea air and see waves. A white lighthouse stands on the cliff above the harbour, built in the 1850s under the Ottomans, and the ruins of an old fort sit on a rock in the bay. The town is known for its hand-woven cotton cloth, Şile bezi, a light, airy fabric that is embroidered and sold in shops along the main street.

Between Istanbul and the coast lies the Belgrad Forest and the wooded hills that supply the city with water, a belt of oak, beech and hornbeam that is cool and shady in summer. The roads that cross it are some of the best riding near the city, with long, smooth bends and little traffic on weekdays. At the coast, the land opens into low cliffs, sandy beaches and fishing villages, and the sea is a darker, rougher blue than the Mediterranean. Ağva, a little further east, is a quiet river village with guesthouses and fish restaurants.

The swim is the point, and on a hot weekend in July or August the beaches are crowded, with families, umbrellas and tea sellers. Water temperatures are cool, and currents and waves can be strong, so respect the flags. On weekdays and in spring and early autumn the beaches are calmer. The town fills with Istanbul day trippers on weekends, so aim to arrive early and leave before the afternoon rush back to the city, which can be heavy.

Şile has fuel stations, restaurants and cafés, and the fresh fish and grilled meatballs are good. Mist or sea fog can roll in without warning, and the coast road can be slippery. Wear a layer, bring cash and enjoy the cool air.
t.shipka pass@42.8,25.3:
Shipka Pass is a modest height, about 1,190 metres, in the Balkan Mountains, but few passes in Europe carry so much memory. In the summer of 1877, during the war between Russia and the Ottoman Empire, a force of Russian soldiers and Bulgarian volunteers held this saddle against repeated attacks by a much larger Ottoman army, and their stand helped open the way to Bulgarian independence a few months later. The fighting was fierce, the casualties heavy, and the winter that followed killed more men from cold than from bullets.

The pass lies in the central Balkan range, which the Bulgarians call Stara Planina, the Old Mountain, and the road across it connects the town of Gabrovo on the northern side with the Valley of Roses and Kazanlak on the south. It is a classic mountain road, climbing through beech forest with tight bends and generous gradients, and the surface is generally decent, though in some places it is patched and rough. It is not a long or difficult pass, but it is a good one, with a quiet rhythm and a lot of green.

The weather is changeable. The ridge catches the weather coming from the north, so fog, cold wind and rain can arrive quickly, even in summer, and snow can lie on the road from late autumn until spring. If the forecast is poor, think about the descent, and take a layer for the top. A clear day brings a view southward over the rose valley, and northward over a rolling country of forest and farms.

The area around the pass is full of monuments, and the road is lined with signs and plaques. Just above the pass you can see the large memorial on Shipka Peak, and further down, in the village of Shipka, there is a Russian church with golden domes. Local shops sell souvenirs, honey and herbs, and there is a small snack bar near the top where you can have a coffee and a pastry.

Fuel is available at Gabrovo, about thirteen kilometres to the north, which is a real town with a long industrial history and a famous museum of humour. On the southern side, Kazanlak is the larger town. In late spring, when the roses begin to bloom in the valley below, this is a lovely time to cross.
t.shipka memorial@42.7,25.3:
The Freedom Monument on Shipka Peak is a tall stone tower on a bare summit, with a bronze lion carved into the base and a wide, wild view in every direction. It stands at about 1,300 metres above the pass, and it was completed in the 1930s to honour the men who fought and died in the defence of Shipka in 1877 and 1878. Reaching the top means climbing a long staircase of some nine hundred steps, which is a serious effort in motorcycle gear, and most riders are content to look at it from the car park and take a few photographs.

The monument commemorates the Russian soldiers and the Bulgarian volunteers, the opalchentsi, who held the pass against Ottoman forces. The peak is named for the Russian general Nikolai Stoletov, who commanded the defence in the first battle, and the Bulgarian volunteers were among the first soldiers of the modern Bulgarian state. In the winter that followed the main fighting, hundreds of Russian soldiers froze to death in their trenches, and the contrast between the quiet green slopes now and the brutal winter of 1877 is difficult to hold in the mind. Inside the monument there is a small hall with names and memorials, and from the top, the view over the Valley of Roses, with its rows of fields and the town of Kazanlak, is magnificent.

The road up from the pass is short and steep, with tight hairpins in the forest, and a surface that has suffered from frost. There is a car park at the foot of the stairs, and a few stalls sell drinks and souvenirs. At weekends and holidays, school groups and veterans' parties gather at the foot of the steps, and on national days, the peak is full of flags and speeches. Weather on the summit is often cold and misty, and the wind can be strong enough to make you lean on the railings.

The forest around the memorial is beech and fir, with some rare plants and a few deer and wild boar that you are unlikely to see. The smell of damp earth and resin is strong after rain. The best time to visit is a clear morning in late spring or early autumn, when the haze has not yet formed and the light is good for photography.

Shipka, about four kilometres from the monument, is a small town with basic facilities, and Gabrovo, fourteen kilometres away, is the nearest large town with proper stations and supermarkets. Take water, wear a layer and give yourself time to take the steps slowly if you do decide to climb them.
t.heinola@61.2,26.0:
Heinola sits on a narrow strip of land between two lakes in southern Finland, about fifty kilometres north-east of Lahti, and it is one of those towns that has quietly reinvented itself more than once. It is a lakeland place through and through, with water on both sides, and the big lake system of Päijänne and the Kymijoki watershed lies close by. The Jyrängönkoski rapids, a short walk from the centre, give the town a pleasant spot to watch the current while you drink coffee.

Finland's roads reward a calm approach. The surfaces are generally excellent, the corners gentle and rolling through spruce and birch forest, and the country is thinly populated enough that you can ride for an hour without seeing much traffic. Speed limits are strictly enforced, with cameras and fines scaled to income, so keep to the posted limits, usually eighty or a hundred kilometres per hour on the open road and lower through villages. The greater danger is wildlife: elk, which Finns call moose, wander across roads at dawn and dusk, particularly in late summer, and hitting one on a bike would be disastrous. Slow down at twilight.

Summer is the season, from late May to August, when the light barely fades and the lakes steam in the early morning. The countryside is dotted with lakeside cottages, many with a sauna on the shore, and the habit of jumping from a hot sauna into cold water is deeply ingrained. Autumn brings colour and quiet, though temperatures drop fast. Finnish law gives everyone the right to roam, and to camp for a night in most woodland as long as you leave no trace, which makes a long ride in the lakelands unusually easy to stretch into an overnight.

Heinola is a good practical stop. With a population of about twenty thousand it has fuel, supermarkets, cafés and a pleasant harbour area, and summer cafés open along the shore. Try a Finnish pastry such as a korvapuusti, the cinnamon bun, with your coffee, or a lunch of vendace or perch if you can find it. Lahti, a larger city, lies down the road to the south-west, and the lakes to the north offer a hundred places to pause.
t.akcakoca side@41.1,29.8:
The coordinates put you on the Black Sea shore in the Ağva district, east of Şile, where two rivers, the Göksu and the Yeşilçay, come down through the forest to the sea and make a small estuary lined with guesthouses. It is a gentle, green stretch of coast, a few hours from the crush of Istanbul and a world apart from it, with wooded hills coming right to the water and long beaches of dark sand where the Black Sea throws surf onto the shore.

The Black Sea coast is not the Mediterranean, and the character here is different: cooler, wetter, more forested. Oak, beech and hornbeam press close to the road, there is mist in the mornings, and the sea is often grey and restless, with a swell that makes swimming a matter of watching the flags. The rivers are slow and brown, and you can take a boat up the Göksu through reed beds and woods, a trip that locals do at weekends. The weather can turn quickly, with cloud rolling in from the sea and showers that leave the roads slick.

For riders, the coast road east of Şile is one of the best easy days in the Istanbul region. It follows the cliffs and coves with a string of bends, with a smooth surface for most of the way, passing through forest, farmland and small fishing villages. Weekend traffic from Istanbul can clog the road near the more popular beaches, particularly in July and August, so aim for an early start or a midweek ride. Watch for wet leaves and sand on the corners, and for the occasional tractor or herd of cows in the villages.

Şile, to the west, is known for its cotton cloth, a loosely woven, embroidered fabric, and for a lighthouse that has watched over the coast since the nineteenth century. Ağva itself, a small town of about nine thousand, has fuel, shops and plenty of places that cook fish and the fried anchovy that the Black Sea does so well. Kandıra, to the east, is the next larger place. Spring and early autumn are the best times to come, when the beaches are quiet and the forest is fresh.
t.sar alan@40.1,29.2:
Sarıalan, the yellow meadow, is the place where the Uludağ road leaves the lower slopes and enters the high forest. It sits at sixteen hundred metres on the northern flank of the mountain above Bursa, a picnic and camping area among tall firs, and for the people of Bursa it is the first breath of cool air on a hot summer weekend. You smell it before you get there: resin, damp earth and the smoke of barbecues.

The mountain is Uludağ, the great mountain, in ancient times known as the Mysian Olympus, and it is the highest peak in the Marmara region at around twenty-five hundred metres. The forest on its slopes is mostly fir, a local variety of the Caucasian fir that grows in the northern mountains of Turkey, with beech and oak lower down and open alpine meadows higher up. In winter the whole mountain is Turkey's best-known ski resort, and in summer it is a cool refuge, with wildflowers in the meadows and mist moving through the trees. A national park protects the best of the upper forest.

The road up from Bursa is one of the great climbs in Turkey, with dozens of bends and hairpins that carry you from the city at a few hundred metres to the ski hotels at nineteen hundred. By the time you pass through Sarıalan you are in the cool, shaded middle section, where the gradient is steady, the surface is mostly good, and the corners are tight enough to keep you busy. Fog and cloud often cover the upper slopes even when Bursa is sunny, and there can be ice on the road well into spring, so dress for the top, not the bottom. In snow, you will need chains, and the road may be closed.

Bursa, in the plain below, was the first capital of the Ottomans, and it is worth a visit for its old bazaars, green-tiled mosques and the famous Iskender kebab, as well as the local sweet of candied chestnuts. For fuel, Kestel and Gürsu, at the foot of the mountain, are both big enough to have stations, and Bursa has everything. There are cafes and small restaurants at Sarıalan and on the way up, with views that improve the tea. Weekends are crowded, so go early on a weekday if you can, and aim for late spring or early autumn.
t.uludag@40.1,29.2:
At nineteen hundred metres, the road gives up and the ski hotels begin. Uludağ is both a mountain and a resort, a cluster of hotels, lifts and restaurants built on the broad shoulder of the peak, with the summit another six hundred metres or so above. In winter this is the busiest ski area in the country, and the slopes are full of people from Istanbul and Bursa; in summer, the hotels are quiet, the meadows are green, and the mountain belongs to hikers and the odd motorcyclist.

The climb is the real event. From Bursa, the road runs up the north face of the mountain in a ceaseless sequence of bends, passing through orchards and chestnut woods, then pine, then the tall firs, before emerging onto the open slopes near the top. The surface is generally well maintained, as you would expect on a road used by skiers, but the gradients are steep and the corners tight, so engine braking and clean lines matter. Fog is common at the top, and temperatures can be many degrees colder than in Bursa, with a biting wind. Even in summer, you may need a warm layer and waterproofs.

The mountain has a history that goes back a very long way. In antiquity it was known as Mount Olympus, the Mysian Olympus, to distinguish it from the one in Greece, and hermits and monks lived in the forests in the Byzantine period, so there is a story to the place beyond the hotels. On clear days, from the summit area you can see across the Marmara Sea and, on a very clear day, the hills around Istanbul, which is a reward worth waiting for. The alpine flora is rich, with flowers appearing as soon as the snow retreats.

Practical matters are straightforward. There is no reliable fuel at the top, so fill up in Bursa or in Kestel, eleven kilometres from the mountain's base. The hotels have restaurants, and there are a handful of cafes and kiosks that serve tea, grilled sandwiches and the sort of hot food that suits the cold. In winter, snow tyres or chains are required on the road, and the surface can be icy. The summer months, from June to September, are the best time for a ride, and midweek is much quieter than the weekends.
t.maki paalys makipallys@60.1,27.0:
The coordinates drop this stop into the Gulf of Finland, south of the port city of Kotka, which means we are among the outer islands of the Kymenlaakso archipelago, where the mainland breaks up into skerries, bare granite and low pine. The name is Finnish for something like a hill with a crest, and the Finnish coast has a lot of those: smooth, ice-scoured rocks rounded by the last glaciation and still rising from the sea by several millimetres a year.

The nearest mainland roads are straightforward and well kept, which is characteristic of Finland. The main road along the coast between Helsinki and the Russian border is fast and busy with trucks, and speed limits drop with the seasons, with winter limits lower than summer ones and cameras in the usual places. The small coast roads, by contrast, run through forest and over the inlets by little bridges, with farms, birch and spruce, and the smell of resin and tar. Moose and deer are a real risk at dawn and dusk, and a collision with a moose is no joke, so slow down when the trees come close to the road.

Summer is the time. Around midsummer it never really gets dark this far north, and the evening light turns long and golden. Mosquitoes can be fierce in July. In the shoulder seasons the Gulf can be grey and moody, and from December the sea freezes near the shore.

Kotka and Hamina are the places for fuel and a proper meal, and every village has a small shop that opens when it suits it. The fishing here is for Baltic herring and perch, and a good local dish is smoked fish with new potatoes and dill. Bring a map or a downloaded route, as the islands are not signed in the way a mainland town would be, and check ferry or boat access before going, because the outer isles are reached only by water.
t.aalto works@61.1,25.0:
Lammi lies in the lake country of southern Finland, in the Häme region, about a hundred kilometres north of Helsinki, and its fame rests on two things: a lake landscape of unusual calm, and a beer. The beer is sahti, a traditional Finnish farmhouse ale brewed from malted barley and rye, flavoured with juniper rather than hops, and filtered through juniper branches. It is cloudy, sweet and surprisingly strong, and Lammi is considered the capital of sahti, with brewers who have kept the tradition alive for generations. A glass, if you can find it, is worth trying, though not before riding.

The label on the map points to Alvar Aalto, Finland's best-known architect, whose buildings are scattered across the country, but I cannot tie a particular building to this spot with certainty, so I will describe the place around it. The landscape is classic Finland: forest of pine and spruce, birch groves, small lakes with reeds and boathouses, and wooden farm buildings painted red or ochre. Nearby is the Evo forest, a large area of old woodland with many lakes, popular for walking and fishing, and the Lammi Biological Station of the University of Helsinki studies the ecosystems of the lakes.

The roads in the area are a pleasure. Narrow, quiet and well surfaced, they curve between lakes and woods, with gentle ups and downs, and the speed limits are strictly enforced, with cameras on the main roads. Deer and elk can cross at dusk, and collisions with elk are a serious hazard in Finland, so watch your speed in the evening and early morning. In summer, the roads are shaded by trees, and the lakes sparkle through the gaps. Autumn is lovely, with golden birch, and the first frost brings a crispness to the air. Winter brings ice and snow, and the riding season ends.

Lammi has about five thousand people, so you will find a fuel station and a small supermarket, and Hämeenkoski and Tuulos are smaller, with limited services. A cup of coffee and a pulla, a cardamom bun, at a village cafe is an ideal stop. The smell of the place is pine resin and lake water, with woodsmoke in the evening. In the summer light, which lasts until almost midnight, a late ride to the lakeshore feels like a gift.
t.istanbul@41.0,29.0:
Istanbul sits across two continents, split by the Bosporus, and the point here is in the old peninsula on the European side, where the Golden Horn meets the strait. The city was Byzantium, then Constantinople, capital of the Roman Empire in the east for over a thousand years, and from 1453 the seat of the Ottoman sultans. The layers show everywhere. Hagia Sophia, finished in 537, still has the most astonishing dome in the world, hung as if from nothing over a vast interior, and nearby the Blue Mosque, with its six minarets and cascade of domes, stands across a garden, built in the early seventeenth century as an Ottoman answer.

The area also holds Topkapı Palace, where sultans lived above the Bosporus, the Basilica Cistern, an underground reservoir with a forest of columns, and the Grand Bazaar, a covered labyrinth of some four thousand shops, selling carpets, ceramics, gold and lamps. At Eminönü, on the water, ferries leave for Kadıköy and the Asian side, and fishermen sell sandwiches of grilled mackerel from boats that rock at the quay. The city is loud, dense and exhausting, and also one of the most rewarding in the world to walk in.

Riding in Istanbul requires a calm head. The traffic is heavy at almost any hour, the lanes are fluid, and delivery riders on small scooters weave through gaps with confidence. The bridges across the Bosporus and the motorways are fast and busy, and the cobbled streets of the old town are steep and slippery when wet. The best time to move is early on a Sunday, when the city is quiet, and a short ferry ride is often a better way to cross than the bridge. In winter, rain and cold wind from the Black Sea are common, and spring and autumn are the pleasant seasons.

Fuel is easy, with stations throughout the city, though they are less common on the old peninsula, and parking for a motorcycle near the sights is limited, so a secure garage is useful. After the sights, a plate of fish at a small meyhane in the back streets, with a glass of raki and a dish of mezes, is the right way to finish a day, and tea in a tulip-shaped glass will arrive without being asked.
t.muradiye@40.2,29.0:
Bursa was the first great capital of the Ottomans, taken in 1326 and held for over a century before the court moved to Edirne, and the Muradiye district is where the sultans of that period are buried. The complex was begun in 1426 by Sultan Murad II, a mosque with a medrese and a garden, and around it are a dozen or so tombs of sultans and their families, set among cypress trees and roses. The tombs are plain from outside and surprisingly lovely inside, with painted ceilings, tiled walls and a row of simple sarcophagi. One of them holds the sons of Mehmed the Conqueror, and the stories of the princes buried here, some of them victims of palace power struggles, have their own sad drama.

The old city lies on the lower slopes of Uludağ, the mountain the ancients called Mount Olympus of Mysia, which rises behind it to over 2,500 metres and holds snow into late spring. Bursa is known for silk, and the Koza Han, a caravanserai from the fifteenth century, still has silk merchants in its courtyard. The Green Mosque and tomb, with their blue-green tiles, and the Ulu Cami, a vast mosque with twenty domes, are close by. Food matters here too. The İskender kebab, sliced lamb on bread with tomato sauce and butter, was invented in the city, and the candied chestnuts, kestane şekeri, are sold in every shop.

The riding is the bonus. From the city the road to the ski resort on Uludağ climbs in long hairpins through forest of beech and fir, rising some 1,500 metres in a few dozen kilometres, with a clean and well-kept surface. The upper reaches are often in cloud, the air at the top is cold even in summer, and snow closes the road in winter or requires chains. Below the city, the plain of Bursa is rich with orchards and mulberry trees, and traffic into and around the city can be heavy, with trucks and buses on the main roads.

Bursa has more than a million people, and so fuel, repairs and food are simple. Cumalıkızık, an Ottoman village with cobbled lanes, lies a short ride to the east and is a pleasant stop for breakfast.
t.kazanlak@42.6,25.4:
In early June the air around Kazanlak smells faintly of roses, and it is no marketing trick. The town of about fifty-five thousand sits in a broad valley between the Balkan range to the north and the lower Sredna Gora to the south, and the fields here have for centuries been planted with the damask rose, whose petals are picked at dawn and distilled into oil that perfumers buy by the gram. The Rose Festival, held in the first weekend of June, fills the streets with parades and folk dancing and a general air of cheerful chaos.

The town carries more history than its modern concrete suggests. On its edge is the Thracian Tomb of Kazanlak, from the fourth century BC, a small beehive chamber painted with vivid scenes of a funeral feast, and it is on the UNESCO list. The original is closed to protect the paintings, but an exact replica stands nearby and is worth the visit. The Thracians were master horsemen and goldsmiths who ruled this region before the Romans, and the valley is dotted with burial mounds that have yielded splendid treasures.

North of town the road climbs into the Balkan range toward the Shipka Pass, which reaches about 1,185 metres. The ascent winds through beech forest in a long series of bends, with good tarmac in most places and a few patches that suffer from frost damage. At the top stands a huge stone memorial to the 1877 to 1878 battles, in which Russian and Bulgarian volunteers held the pass against Ottoman attacks during the war that led to Bulgarian independence. The monument on Stoletov peak is reached by a long staircase, and the view south over the valley of roses is wide. Near the foot, the church of the Nativity, with its gold-topped domes, belongs to the Russian monastery at Shipka and glitters through the trees.

Fuel is easy, as Kazanlak is a real town with several stations, supermarkets and cafes. Bulgarian food is simple and good, with shopska salad, grilled meat and a very strong coffee, and prices are modest.

The pass can be wet and foggy at any time, and snow closes it in deep winter. The best months are May, June and September, when the days are warm and the valley is green.
t.kuopio@62.9,27.7:
Kuopio is a lakeside city in the middle of eastern Finland, a place of just under ninety thousand people spread between water and forest, and it is the capital of the Savo region, whose people are known for their sense of humour and their talkative, roundabout way of speaking. The town stands on the shore of Lake Kuopio, one of thousands of lakes in this part of the country, and in summer, the water is dotted with boats and the air is full of birdsong. In winter, the lake freezes, and the people skate and ski across it.

Above the city rises the Puijo hill, with a concrete tower, about seventy-five metres high, which holds a viewing platform and a restaurant. On a clear day, the panorama over the lakes, islands and forests of the Savo is endless, a landscape of blue and green that stretches to every horizon. In the town itself, the market square is the heart of the city, selling berries, fresh fish and a local speciality called kalakukko, a loaf of rye bread baked with fish and pork inside, which is eaten warm or cold and is sold in bakeries all over the region. The Orthodox church museum and the neoclassical cathedral are small but pleasant.

The ride leads to Petäjävesi, a village about a hundred kilometres to the south-west, where an old wooden church, built in the 1760s by a local carpenter family, stands among pines. It has been on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 1994, and its simple log walls and steep shingled roof show how Finnish timber building mixed Lutheran sobriety with a touch of the baroque. The church is a modest building, but it feels very genuine.

The roads in Finland are well maintained, and the traffic is light, but the great danger is the elk, a huge animal that can cause serious accidents. It is most active at dusk and dawn, particularly from late summer, so it pays to ride carefully and watch the verges. Speed limits are strict, and fines depend on income. In midsummer, the sun hardly sets, and daylight lasts nearly all night.

Fuel is easy in Kuopio, with stations on the main roads and supermarkets in the centre, but in the countryside, stations may be far apart, so fill up regularly. The season for motorcycling is short, from May to September, and the best weather is in July.
t.savonlinna@61.9,28.9:
Savonlinna rises out of the water in the middle of Finland's Lake Saimaa, a town of just over twenty-seven thousand built across islands and narrow straits, with the great stone castle of Olavinlinna holding the centre. The fortress was founded in 1475 by Erik Axelsson Tott, a Swedish-Finnish knight, to guard the eastern border against Novgorod and Russia, and it has been bashed about by wars ever since. Today it hosts the Savonlinna Opera Festival each July, when thousands of people sit in the courtyard to hear arias echo off medieval walls. It is one of the odder pleasures of the Nordic summer.

The landscape here is lakes and more lakes, with forested islands, eskers and thin ridges, all left behind by the retreating ice sheet. Saimaa has its own population of ringed seals, one of the rarest in the world, and in the long Finnish summer light the water seems to glow late into the night. Locals eat vendace, small fried muikku, and a sweet pastry called lörtsy, filled with meat or jam, is a Savonlinna speciality you can try at a lakeside kiosk.

As for riding, the roads here are quiet, smooth and relaxed. The famous Punkaharju ridge road to the east runs along a narrow esker with water on both sides, lined with tall pines, and it feels like riding along the top of a wall. Corners are gentle, speeds are enforced strictly, and the main hazards are elk and reindeer at dusk, plus the occasional lorry carrying timber. Kerimäki, about twenty kilometres east, has a huge wooden church, said to be the largest of its kind in the world, whose scale seems out of proportion to the village.

Savonlinna itself has all the services you would need. Fuel stations are easy to find, the market square by the harbour has coffee and pastries, and there are plenty of spots for a longer lunch. In summer the town is busy, particularly during the opera weeks, so book accommodation ahead. The best times to ride are June to August, and mornings are cool and calm. In September the birch leaves turn yellow, and the roads empty.
t.fayetteville arkansas@36.1,-94.2:
Fayetteville sits on the northern shoulder of the Boston Mountains, the highest and roughest part of the Ozarks, and it behaves like a college town that happens to be surrounded by hills. The University of Arkansas gives the place its energy, its Dickson Street bars and its autumn Saturdays, when the whole town seems to dress in cardinal red for the Razorbacks. With more than eighty thousand people it has every kind of fuel, food and bike shop you could want, so a ride that starts and ends here never has to worry about logistics.

The point of leaving is the land to the south. Once you clear the last strip malls, the roads begin to rise and fall over ridges that never get very high but rarely stay flat. Most of the interesting roads are two-lane state highways wrapped around hollows, with tight little bends, blind crests and the odd cattle guard. The famous one is the Pig Trail, Highway 23, which runs south through the Ozark National Forest toward Ozark and the Arkansas River valley. It is narrow in places, shaded by oak and hickory, and a long way from anywhere you could call fast.

Timing matters. October is the headline, when the hardwoods turn and the weekend traffic of motorcycles on that road is thick enough that locals plan around it. Spring brings dogwood and redbud along the verges, and summer is hot, humid and loud with cicadas. Gravel does wash across the apex after heavy rain, and deer are an everyday hazard at dusk, so the best light is mid-morning to mid-afternoon.

The country itself has a quiet story. Cherokee people were driven through this corner of the Ozarks on their way west, and the Civil War's Battle of Prairie Grove, a short ride southwest, still marks the ground with a state park. Closer to town, Mount Sequoyah gives you a view over the valley and the university from the north side, while the old railroad corridor has become a paved trail that bypasses the traffic entirely.

Before you head out, top up here rather than counting on the small towns beyond Winslow, where stations are fewer and close early. A proper breakfast on the square, a look at the weather radar, and you are ready for the hills.
t.harrison@36.2,-93.1:
Harrison is the main town of the north Arkansas Ozarks, a courthouse square with a few brick buildings, a lot of pickup trucks and a pace that tells you the big cities are a long way off. It is the seat of Boone County and sits on a plateau above the valley of the Buffalo River, which flows east for well over a hundred miles through limestone bluffs and is protected as the first national river in the United States, set aside in 1972.

Highway 7 reaches Harrison at the northern end of one of the best-known scenic roads in Arkansas, and getting here is the reward for a long day in the hills. Coming up from Jasper, the road passes through Ozark National Forest and drops into the Boxley Valley, a pastoral stretch of the Buffalo where wild elk graze on the open fields near Ponca, a herd that was reintroduced in the 1980s. Autumn is brilliant with maples and hickories, and spring brings green so fresh it looks painted.

The riding on the approach is varied. Some stretches are tight and steep with blind curves, while others open into wide farmland where pastures roll along ridge tops. The road surface is generally decent, but there are tight gravel shoulders, loose gravel at corners and deer that ignore all rules. Early morning and late afternoon are the best times for light, though the animal risk is higher at dusk.

Harrison has all the services you would expect from a town of thirteen thousand. There are fuel stations on the main roads, family restaurants, motels and a good grocery, and it is the best place to resupply before heading further into the hills. Nearby towns like Green Forest and Jasper are far smaller and have limited hours, so fill your tank here.

The town's history is more complicated than its quiet square suggests. Harrison was the site of racial violence in the early twentieth century, and the community has been working in recent decades to confront that past. It is a reminder that the roads we love run through places with real stories, and that a ride is more than the pavement.
t.polonezkoy forest@41.1,29.2:
Polonezkoy is a small village hidden in the forests on Istanbul's Anatolian side, a short way from the chaos of the city and a world apart. It was founded in 1842, when Prince Adam Czartoryski, a Polish aristocrat in exile in Paris, bought land here and offered it to Polish refugees after the failed uprisings against Russian rule, and the village was originally called Adampol. For a long time, its inhabitants spoke Polish and kept their Catholic customs, and the traces still show in the wooden houses with steep roofs, the small chapel and a handful of restaurants serving Polish dishes alongside Turkish ones.

As the start and finish of a ride, it is a refuge. The surrounding forest of oak, beech and hornbeam is protected as a nature park, and the lanes leading in are narrow, shaded and quiet on weekdays, with gentle curves and a surface that varies from smooth to patched. Weekends are another matter: Istanbulites flock here for breakfast and walks, and the road can fill with cars and motorbikes, so early starts are best. Heading north toward the Black Sea, the road continues through more forest, with long, easy bends and occasional views of reservoirs, before dropping to the coast near Sile. The nearest districts with fuel and services are Sancaktepe, Umraniye and Atasehir, about a dozen kilometres away, so fill the tank before heading in.

The village's character comes from its mixed heritage. For generations, it was a place where Polish descendants lived in the Ottoman and later Turkish world, and the community has shrunk as families moved to the city, but a few still live here and keep the old houses. The local cooking is a pleasure: a long country breakfast with eggs, honey, cheeses, olives and fresh bread is a weekend ritual. Polish dishes, such as pierogi and smoked meats, appear on menus.

The forests here are part of a green belt that surrounds Istanbul on both sides of the Bosphorus, and they provide the city with much of its clean air and water. Squirrels, foxes, wild boar and many species of birds live among the trees, and in autumn the leaves turn gold and copper, while in spring the ground is covered in wildflowers. The air smells of damp earth and leaf mould, and after the city's roar the quiet is striking.

Bring a light jacket, since the forest is cooler than the city, and allow plenty of time for the return to Istanbul, where traffic can be heavy.
t.lahti@61.0,25.7:
Lahti sits on the southern shore of Lake Vesijärvi, at the end of a long ridge, and its look was shaped by ice. The ridge is the Salpausselkä, a great curved moraine pushed up at the edge of the retreating glacier about eleven thousand years ago, and it runs across southern Finland like a stone eyebrow. Lahti grew up where the railway and the ridge met, a young city by Finnish standards, officially a town only since 1905, and it has become one of the country's winter sports centres. The big ski-jumping hills dominate the skyline, with the Lahti Ski Games held every winter, and a museum tells the history.

The city has about ninety-eight thousand people, plenty of fuel, shops and services, and a cheerful, practical air. Its greatest building is the Sibelius Hall, a timber-and-glass concert hall on the lakeshore that opened in 2000, with a vast wooden interior, and the harbour has boats in summer and ice in winter. A radio and television museum and a small harbour market round out the sights. Try a Karelian pie, with rice porridge and egg butter, or a bowl of salmon soup, creamy and mild, at the market hall.

The riding in the Finnish Lakeland is slow and meditative, and it should be approached in that spirit. Roads run between lakes, forests of pine and spruce, birch groves and open farmland, with water appearing every few minutes, and the surfaces are generally smooth. Corners are gentle, speed limits are modest, and the police use cameras and patrol cars, so keep to them. The long ridge of the Salpausselkä rolls the road up and down in a pleasant rhythm. Nearby Päijänne, the second-largest lake in Finland, has a long, deep, island-studded shore.

Elk and reindeer cross roads at dusk and dawn, and a collision with one is serious, so watch the verges and slow down in forest. In June and July, the nights are so light that you can ride almost round the clock, though fatigue is a danger. The mosquitoes arrive in July, so keep repellent in your pocket. Summer weather is mild, with occasional rain, and autumn colours in September are splendid. Lahti is a fine place to begin, with a hearty breakfast and a full tank.
Past Cass the road finally starts to do what its reputation promises. The forest closes in, the hills steepen, and Highway 23 begins to wind through a run of tight, banked hairpins that climb and drop through deep hardwood forest, with the Mulberry River tucked away on the left in a rocky valley. This is the Boston Mountains, the highest and roughest part of the Ozarks, a plateau cut by streams into a maze of steep ridges and hollows, and the forest of oak, hickory and maple is among the most extensive in the central United States.

Riding here is a pleasure that needs some attention. The corners come in sequences, some tight, some open, and the surface is usually good, though it can be strewn with sand, gravel and leaves, especially after rain. Blind bends are common, and local riders and cars often cut the centre line, so stay to your side and look through the turn. The road is also popular with cyclists, and on a fall weekend, it can fill with riders from dawn to dusk. The speed limit is modest and police patrols are frequent, so the best approach is to ride fluidly and enjoy the rhythm.

The Mulberry is a designated National Wild and Scenic River, and a favourite among canoeists and kayakers, who run it in spring when the rain has filled it. A small store at one of the river crossings sells snacks, drinks and gifts, and serves as a meeting point for riders, and in season you can sit on its porch with a cold drink and watch the traffic. Stop and ask the locals about the best loop roads, because they know them well.

Fuel is not available along this stretch. Ozark lies about twenty-three kilometres south, and the next real supply to the north is in Fayetteville or Huntsville, so check your tank. Cell coverage is patchy in the hollows. Carry some water, a basic tool kit and a tyre repair kit.

Autumn is the peak season. The forest turns red, orange and gold in mid to late October, and the smell of leaf litter and woodsmoke follows you through the bends. In spring the dogwoods bloom white in the understory, and the creeks run high. Summer is green and humid, and a cool breeze in the hollows is a relief. Keep an eye on the sky, because storms can build quickly.
Further north, the Boston Mountains begin to relax. The ridges flatten into a broad plateau, the hairpins ease into longer, smoother bends, and the road settles into a gentle rhythm through deep hardwood forest with occasional clearings for farms, hay meadows and small chapels. The nearest towns, Huntsville and Elkins, lie off to the north and west, and between them is some of the quietest country in Arkansas.

The forest here is an important and beautiful one. The Ozark National Forest covers more than a million acres of oak, hickory and shortleaf pine, and the rocks beneath are mostly sandstone and limestone, which dissolve slowly into caves, springs and sinkholes. Black bears, wiped out in the region by the early twentieth century, were reintroduced from Minnesota in the 1950s and 60s, and today the Arkansas Ozarks hold a healthy population. Wild turkeys, white-tailed deer and, in the creeks, small fish and crayfish are all present, though bears are rarely seen from the road.

The road itself is a joy for a relaxed rider. The surface is generally well kept, and the traffic is light on weekdays. The curves are long and open, often with good sight lines, which allows a smooth, easy pace. The stretch is also a fine place to look at the details: the moss on the roadside rocks, the creek crossings, the old stone walls and the mailboxes made from milk churns. The Arkansas Ozarks have a handful of old general stores, and some of them still serve a plate of biscuits and gravy, or a slice of pie and a coffee.

Fuel is the main practical concern. There are no stations in this stretch of forest, and the nearest, in Huntsville, Elkins or Ozark, lie more than thirty kilometres away. Keep the tank above half, and carry water and snacks, because the road can be empty for long periods. A wrong turn onto a forest road can end in gravel or mud, so stay on the signed highway unless your bike is built for it.

Spring and fall are the best seasons for the ride. In April, redbud and dogwood bloom, and in October the colours are spectacular. Summer is hot and humid, with thunderstorms in the afternoon, and winter brings occasional ice on the shaded bends. If you are heading north toward Fayetteville, the route eases into a more open landscape of pasture and small towns.
